Beginning at 5th level, you can attack twice, instead of once, whenever you take the Attack action on your turn. Additionally, attacks from your mounted weapons count as magical for the purposes of overcoming resistance and immunity to nonmagical attacks and damage.
At 9th level, you’re able to fit more modifications on your vehicle. You may now have two specialized modifications and two mounted weapons active at once.

At 15th level, you learn to overclock your vehicle to force it to perform past its peak temporarily. As a bonus action, you can send your vehicle into overdrive for one minute. Doing so doubles its movement speed, makes it immune to all damage, and allows you to make up to three attacks with your mounted weapon each turn. At the end of the minute, your vehicle is immediately destroyed. You must finish a long rest to use this feature again, unless you spend a spell slot of 5th level or higher to use it again.
Harbingers are foretellers of death and destruction, serving as a warning for disaster and ruin. Oftentimes, they take it upon themselves to cause the catastrophes themselves.

At 3rd level, you learn the toll the dead and sacred flame cantrips, which counts as a spiritualist cantrip for you. When you cast a spiritualist cantrip, the DC is equal to your Art save DC. Whenever you activate your spirit tether, the target has disadvantage on the saving throw against spiritualist cantrips you cast until the end of your turn.
Also at 3rd level, you gain access to new spirit arts that reflect your penchant for bringing about tragedy.

As an action, you can spend 1 spirit point to attempt to imbue your target with a Suffering mark. The target must make a Wisdom saving throw or be marked and take 2d6 necrotic damage. Whenever you cast a spiritualist cantrip on the marked target, you may trigger this spirit art’s effect again without spending spirit points.

As an action, you can spend 1 spirit point to attempt to imbue your target with a Ruination mark. The target must make an Intelligence saving throw or be marked and subtract 1d6 from each saving throw it makes against your harbinger arts or spiritualist cantrips until the end of its next turn. Whenever you cast a spiritualist cantrip on the marked target, you may trigger this spirit art’s effect again without spending spirit points.

As an action, you can spend 1 spirit point to attempt to imbue your target with a Tragedy mark. The target must make a Charisma saving throw or take 1d6 psychic damage each time it attacks or casts a spell until the end of its next turn. Whenever you cast a spiritualist cantrip on the marked target, you may trigger this spirit art’s effect again without spending spirit points.
At 6th level, whenever the target of your spiritualist cantrips has a Suffering, Ruination, and Tragedy mark, you can add an additional 2 damage dice to the cantrip’s damage roll.

At 13th level, you find new ways of inflicting woe upon foes. The damage from your Suffering and Tragedy marks increase by 2d6. In addition, when a target fails its saving throw against one of your marks, you can consume the mark. The mark is removed from the target, and you regain 2d6 hit points.
At 18th level, you master your prowess at bestowing tribulation. You learn the following spirit art:

As an action, you can spend 5 spirit points to imbue your target with a Calamity mark. The target must make a Constitution saving throw or be marked, taking 4d6 force damage and suffering one level of exhaustion. Whenever you cast a spiritualist cantrip on the marked target, you may trigger this spirit art’s effect again without spending spirit points. This mark can count as a Suffering, Ruination, or Tragedy mark for the purposes of satisfying the requirements of your enervating marks feature, but only one of the three at a time.

Throughout the continent of kara-tur, one mineral stands above all else in terms of status. Where in the west you would display decadence with gold, in the east, the truest symbol of power is jade. Legends tell of warriors embellished with regality, often proud in status and seeped in regality. The Jade Lords of Shou Lung were legendary figures that displayed power and wealth in equal measure, fighting with both honor and flair.

Even at 3rd level, you carry yourself with grace and nobility. You gain proficiency in either Persuasion or Intimidation. If you already have both of those proficiencies, you can choose a different proficiency instead.

At 3rd level, the gutteral flow of combat splinters jade around you. When you hit a creature with a weapon attack or a creature hits you with an attack, a jade shard splinters off of you and orbits you for the duration. You can only have a number of jade shards equal to half your fighter level (rounded up) at a time. When initiative ends, any remaining jade shards drop to the floor and disappear. You can expend any number of these shards to take special actions called jade tricks. If the trick requires the target to make a saving throw, the DC is calculated as follows: Jade Trick DC = 8 + your proficiency bonus + your Strength or Dexterity modifier (your choice) If you’re able to make multiple attacks with the Attack action, a trick replaces one of them. You can only use a trick once per attack action.

Make a melee attack with a melee weapon you are holding against a target within range. On a hit, the target suffers the weapon attack’s normal effects and takes a number of d6s in additional damage equal to the amount of shards spent.
Make a ranged or thrown weapon attack (your choice) against a target within 120 feet of you. The attack deals a number of d8s of piercing damage equal to the amount of shards spent.
Choose a point you can see within 60 feet of you. Creatures within 10 feet of that point must make a Dexterity saving throw or take a number of d10s in slashing damage equal to the jade shards spent.
At 7th level, the jade you create is fortified. Damage from jade tricks count as magical for the purposes of overcoming resistance and immunity to non-magical damage.

At 10th level, you learn to pull in the jade shards orbiting you to use as armor. As a bonus action, you can expend any number of jade shards to create jade armor. While this armor is active, you have half cover, or 3/4ths cover if you spent five or more shards. This armor lasts for a number of rounds equal to the jade shards spent or until the end of initiative.

At 15th level, you are able to protect allies with your jade armor as well. If any ally is attacked or is forced to roll a saving throw, you can use your reaction to expend any amount of jade shards and encase them in jade armor. This armor confers the same amount of cover as your jade armor feature, but only lasts until the end of that ally’s next turn.
At 18th level, you learn a new jade trick.

By expending any amount of jade shards, you can create a jadestorm around you in a 20 foot radius, designating any creatures you wish to be unaffected by it. The storm travels with you, with its area being lightly obscured. An affected creature that begins its turn within the jadestorm takes bludgeoning, piercing, and slashing damage equal to the shards expended. Additionally, their AC is reduced by half the expended amount (rounded down) until the start of their next turn or until they leave the jadestorm. The jadestorm lasts for the expended amount of rounds or until the end of initiative.

While in many cases using heavier two-handed weapons would put the user at a disadvantage defensively, Juggernauts utilize this augment to their offensive capabilities to compliment their defenses with little tradeoff. Features: 3rd Level - Martial Training 3rd Level - Defensive Battering 5th Level - Crushing Force 13th Level - Demolishing Stance 18th Level - Raw Terror
When you select this specialization at 3rd level, you gain proficiency in martial weapons.
Additionally at 3rd level, you have the ability to use larger weapons to block and deflect incoming attacks. While you are wielding a weapon with two hands, you gain a +1 bonus to your armor class.

Starting at 7th level, the sheer force you deliver with your attacks is enough to shatter your foe’s defenses. When you hit a creature with a weapon attack, you can reduce the effectiveness of their armor, if they are wearing any, reducing their armor class by 3. Shields, and armor created by spells or other magic are unaffected, and you cannot reduce a creature’s armor class below what it would be without armor. This reduction lasts until the end of the creature’s next turn.

When you reach 13th level, your martial capability reaches new heights in conjunction with your defenses. While your defensive Stance is active, you gain a bonus to damage rolls with weapons equal to the armor class bonus given to you by your stance.

At 18th level, your very presence strikes terror into your foes. While your defensive stance is active, you can use a bonus action to force each creature of your choice within 30 feet of you to make a wisdom saving throw (DC 8 + your strength modifier + your proficiency bonus) or be frightened of you for one minute. An affected creature can repeat this save at the end of each of its turns, ending the effect on a successful save. Once you use this feature, you cannot do so again until you take up a new defensive stance.
The oath was never the end of it. It was the apprenticeship. Prerequisites: Paladin 20 As a Justiciar, you gain the following features.
You gain proficiency in two skills of your choice from the Paladin skill list.

Additionally when you take this prestige class, you gain an increased capacity for spellcasting. You now use half your prestige level (rounded up) on the generic spellcaster level table when determining the amount of spell slots you have available. When you prepare spells for the day, you may now prepare a number of spells equal to half your prestige level + your Charisma modifier. When preparing spells, you now have access to the Cleric spell list for your 6th- to 9th-level spells. You must have spell slots of the spell's level in order to prepare it as normal.
At 21st level, you learn one cantrip of your choice from the Cleric spell list. These cantrips count as Paladin/Justiciar spells for you, and Charisma is your spellcasting ability for them.
At 21st level, you gain twice the number of uses of your Divine Sense feature.

At 21st level, your blessed touch can heal wounds better than before. Your pool of healing power is instead a total number that is now equal to your prestige level x 5. As an action, you can touch a creature and draw power from that pool to restore a number of hit points to that creature, up to a maximum amount remaining in your pool. When expending the last point in your healing pool to do so, it will heal that creature by the maximum number of hit dice that creature has. Additionally, in exchange for one of your attacks during an Attack action you may use Lay on Hands targeting yourself only; doing it this way takes 2 points per 1 hit point healed. Alternatively, you can expend 5 hit points from your pool of healing to cure the target of one disease or neutralize one poison affecting it. You can cure multiple diseases and neutralize multiple poisons with a single use of Lay on Hands II, expending hit points separately for each one. Alternatively, you can expend 10 hit points from your pool of healing to cure the target of one condition affecting it. You can cure multiple conditions with a single use of Lay on Hands, expending hit points separately for each one. Alternatively, you can expend 20 points to remove 1 level of exhaustion from a willing creature.

Starting at 22nd level, this feature replaces your Paladin's 2nd-level Divine Smite feature. When you hit a creature with a melee weapon attack, you can expend one spell slot to deal radiant damage to the target, in addition to the weapon's damage. The extra damage is now 3d8 for a 1st-level spell slot, plus 1d8 for each spell level higher than 1st, to a maximum of 8d8. The damage increases by 3d8 if the target is an undead or a fiend, to a maximum of 11d8. This feature counts as Divine Smite for prerequisites and interactions with other class or subclass features.

When you reach 23rd level, you reaffirm your prior oath and swear another oath that binds you as a Justiciar forever. Up to this time, you have been faithfully carrying out your former oath. Now you rededicate yourself to your former oath, and swear another paladin's oath. Choose from the list of available oaths. Your choice grants you features at 23rd, 27th, 35th, and 40th level.
By 23rd level, the divine magic flowing through you makes you immune to the Poisoned condition and grants you resistance to poison damage.
At 23rd level, you gain one additional use of your Channel Divinity per rest.
When you reach 24th level, you gain the Ability Score Improvement feat or another feat of your choice for which you qualify. You gain this feature again at Justiciar levels 28, 32, 36, and 39.
At 25th level, you can attack three times instead of twice whenever you take the Attack action on your turn.
At 26th level, the range of your Aura of the Guardian extends to 40 feet.
At 27th level, the range of all your Paladin subclass auras extends to 40 feet.
At 30th level, creatures retain the effects of your Aura of Courage for 1 round after leaving it. At 38th level, this extends to 1 minute after leaving your aura.

By 31st level, you are so suffused with righteous might that all your melee weapon strikes carry divine power with them. Whenever you hit a creature with a melee weapon, the creature takes an extra 2d10 radiant damage instead of 1d8.

At 34th level, you can, as a reaction, reflect 1st- and 2nd-level spells back at their caster for a charge of Cleansing Touch. For each additional charge used, this increases the maximum level by 2, up to a maximum of 8th level. This use of Cleansing Touch is a reaction. You may now use your Cleansing Touch feature as a bonus action, and you gain a number of uses of that feature equal to your Charisma modifier (minimum of one).
At 38th level, extend the range of any and all auras from your Paladin/Justiciar class, or its subclasses, to 50 feet.

At 40th level, when you activate one of your 20th-level subclass features that requires activation, you may also activate your other 20th-level subclass feature (should it require activation). Both last for the longer of the two features' durations.

Description You master the physician's arts, gaining the following benefits: Increase your Wisdom score by 1, to a maximum of 20. You gain proficiency in the Medicine skill. If you are already proficient in the skill, you add double your proficiency bonus to checks you make with it. During a short rest, you can clean and bind the wounds of up to six willing beasts, fey, and humanoids. Make a DC 15 Wisdom (Medicine) check for each creature. On a success, if a creature spends a Hit Die during this rest, that creature can forgo the roll and instead regain the maximum number of hit points the die can restore. A creature can do so on a number of Hit Dice equal to half your Wisdom modifier, regardless of how many Hit Dice it spends.
Mediums are the bridge between life and death, often treading over the gap between the two. They call forth spirits of the past, using them for power and knowledge.

At 3rd level, you are able to tap into knowledge from spirits that you know of. You learn speak with dead and can cast it only as if it were a ritual spell. Rather than targeting a corpse, you can speak the name of a deceased individual who died within 1 mile. If their soul is able, they can choose to manifest in an empty space within 5 feet of you and answer your questions. Once a soul is manifested in this way, you can’t manifest the same soul again for 24 hours.
Also at 3rd level, you gain access to new spirit arts that reflect your capacity to channel souls.

As an action, you can spend 1 spirit point to channel the spirit of a warrior. The spirit manifests as a spectral fighter that is always 5 feet away from your target. Whenever you activate your spirit tether, you can have the warrior strike at the target in the same action. The target must succeed on a Dexterity saving throw or take 2d6 force damage. If you use this spirit art again on the same target, you can channel another warrior, up to a maximum of 3 total. Each new warrior increases the force damage dealt to the target by an extra 2d6.

As an action, you can spend 1 spirit point to channel the spirit of a trickster. The spirit manifests in the form of an imp, fairy, or any other tricky creature that is always 5 feet away from your target. Whenever you activate your spirit tether, you can have the trickster distract at the target in the same action. The target must succeed on a Wisdom saving throw or have disadvantage on attack rolls and Perception checks until the end of its next turn.

As an action, you can spend 1 spirit point to channel the spirit of a guardian. The spirit manifests as an ancestor, patron, or angel that is always within 5 feet of you. Whenever you activate your spirit tether, the guardian bestows 1d6 temporary hit points to you. If you use this spirit art again, you can channel another guardian, up to a maximum of 3 total. Each new guardian increases the temporary hit points gained by an extra 1d6.

At 6th level, your frequent interactions with other spirits has strengthened your own considerably. The range of your spirit tether increases to 300 feet. In addition, if your tether breaks while you have at least one active spirit art, you regain one spirit point.

At 13th level, by drawing upon the experiences of the dead, you become temporarily able to utilize their skills. If you make a skill check in any skill you’re not proficient in, you can spend a spirit point to add your proficiency bonus to the roll. You can use this feature after the roll is made, but only before you know the results.
At 18th level, you master your influence over the souls of others. You learn the following spirit art:

If your target is a creature, you can use an action and spend 5 spirit points to attempt to possess them temporarily. The target must succeed on a Charisma saving throw or be possessed by you for a minute. During this time, your soul is transferred into the target’s form, and your original body is left paralyzed. You now control the body but you don’t deprive the target of awareness. You use the possessed target’s statistics, but you retain your alignment, Wisdom, Intelligence, and Charisma. You don’t gain access to the target’s knowledge, class features, or proficiencies. You may end the possession at any time, upon which you return to your body without harm. At the end of each of their turns, the target can repeat the Charisma save, ending the possession on a success. If the target dies while you possess it, your soul is returned to your body without harm. However, if your body dies while possessing the target, the possession ends and you die.

Oracles are seers, soothsayers, and augurs, glimpsing into the future and oftentimes attempting to shape it. Whether your goal lies in preventing horrid events or keeping the future pure and unadulterated, an oracle bears the responsibility of influencing fate itself.
At 3rd level, you are able to predict the future to an extent. You can cast augury at will, using your spiritual focus in place of material components.

At 3rd level, you can subtly tug on the strings of fate to lessen the burden on your allies. Whenever you activate your spirit tether, you can choose whether to deal damage to a target or give them an equal amount of temporary hit points. These temporary hit points disappear if the tether breaks.

Also at 3rd level, you gain access to new spirit arts that reflect your ability to shape the future. Predestined Strike​ When your linked target hits with an attack, you can use your reaction to spend 1 spirit point and choose between these options: Fortune. Roll a d20. On a roll of 10 or above, the attack becomes a critical hit. Disaster. Roll a d20. On a roll of 10 or below, the attack becomes a critical miss. Eyes of Prescience​ You can use an action and spend 1 spirit point to forsee any harm that might befall your target. Choose between these options: Fortune. Until the beginning of your next turn, attack rolls against your target have disadvantage and the target makes Dexterity saving throws with advantage. Disaster. Until the beginning of your next turn, the first attack roll against your target each turn has advantage. Rewound Wounds​ When you activate your spirit tether, you can spend 1 spirit point to use the following effects: Fortune. If your target has taken damage within the last round, you can restore their hit points equal to 2d6 + your wisdom modifier, up to the total damage taken. Disaster. If your target has had hit points restored or has gained temporary hit points within the last round, you can deal necrotic damage equal to 2d6 + your wisdom modifier up to the amount healed or the temporary hit points gained.

At 6th level, your experience with fortune telling allows you to gain a deeper insight into the emotional states of others. While tethered to a creature, you gain an understand of their emotions, giving you insight into fine details. You know how they feel about their current situation, how they react to events that transpire around them, and are able to recognize how they feel about other people, yourself included.

At 13th level, fate bows to your will. If you or an ally within 30 feet misses with an attack roll or fails an ability check or saving throw, you can use your reaction to allow that ally to reroll, potentially succeeding. The ally must use the new roll. You can only use this feature once per short rest, unless you spend 3 spirit points to use it again.

At 18th level, you master your influnece over controlling fate. You learn the following spirit art: Divergence​ If your tethered target becomes critical (10% or fewer hit points) or dies, you can use your reaction to spend 5 spirit points and use one of the following effects: Fortune. You can shift fate so that such an event never occured. If dead, the target is brought back to life, all conditions on the tethered target are ended, and it regains 50 hit points. Disaster. You can use the event to spell disaster for enemies. Tethered targets of your choice take 50 force damage and must succeed on a Charisma saving throw or be stunned. If this damage reduces the target to 0 hit points, the target is disintegrated along with every nonmagical object it is wearing or carrying. Each successful use of this spirit art each day increases its chance to fail by 33%. After three sucessful uses of this spirit art, further uses will fail automatically.

“Roads are for people who already know where they’re going.” The Pathfinder is the one who goes first. Where the maps end, where the trail is cold, where the pass is choked with something that eats scouting parties — that is where a Pathfinder is sent, and where a Pathfinder comes back from. They are the marriage of the soldier and the tracker: the discipline, footwork, and weapon craft of a veteran warrior welded to the instincts of a hunter who has never lost a foe. Armies follow the lines they draw. Caravans survive the passes they clear. Things that hide in the deep places have learned to move when a Pathfinder takes an interest.

Level 20 Cycle: Ranger 7+, Fighter 7+ The cycle must consist of exactly 20 levels split between Ranger and Fighter only, with at least 7 levels in each (e.g. 10/10, 13/7, 7/13). No other class levels may appear in the cycle. Ranger Version: This prestige class is built on X’s Revised (Again) Ranger. Its features assume the Favored Foe and Warden Specialization systems from that revision. Hit Die: 1d10 per Pathfinder level

You gain proficiency in Wisdom (Survival) and Wisdom (Perception). If you are already proficient in one or both, you gain Expertise in it instead, doubling your proficiency bonus for ability checks using it. You can also choose one other skill from the Ranger or Fighter skill list, gaining proficiency in it.

This class is measured in Pathfinder Levels (PfL), numbered 1 through 20 as you advance in it. Your Prestige Level (PL) is always 20 + your Pathfinder Level — it exists to describe your total standing among prestige classes and is what features in this class mean when they scale off “your Prestige Level” (Prestige Level 21 through 40, matching PfL 1 through 20). Your Pathfinder Save DC is 8 + your Proficiency Bonus + your Wisdom modifier.

Your Ranger spellcasting continues past where your qualifying cycle left off, keyed to your Ranger levels rather than your total character level. Calculate your Effective Caster Level: your Ranger levels + your Pathfinder Level (PfL), to a maximum of 33. A 7th-level Ranger entering this class at PfL 1 has an Effective Caster Level of 8; a 13th-level Ranger entering at PfL 1 has an Effective Caster Level of 14. Either way, your first Pathfinder level always picks up exactly one step past where your Ranger spellcasting left off, and every Pathfinder level thereafter advances it by one more — a 13th-level Ranger reaches the table’s cap of 33 at PfL 20, no matter how it’s split. Consult the Pathfinder Ascendant Casting table below using your Effective Caster Level. This replaces your Ranger slots and Spells Known entirely — don’t stack it with your base Ranger table. Wisdom remains your spellcasting ability. As normal, whenever you gain a Pathfinder level you can swap one Ranger spell you know for another.

Rows 8–20 are the standard Ranger half-caster progression, unchanged. From 21 onward this class never opens a 6th-level slot — Spells Known and your existing slots keep widening instead, topping out at 33, the highest Effective Caster Level any Pathfinder can reach (a 13th-level Ranger at Pathfinder Level 20), with a final spread of 7/6/6/5/5 slots and 20 Spells Known. When your Favored Foe dies, you can use a Reaction to designate a new creature within 60 feet as your Favored Foe. You can also designate a creature whose tracks or remains you have examined within the last hour, even if you cannot see it. Your attack bonus against your Favored Foe is equal to your Wisdom modifier (minimum +2), if it is not already. Once per turn when you hit your Favored Foe with a weapon attack, it takes extra damage equal to one roll of your Trailblazer Die. While your Favored Foe is on the same plane of existence, you know its direction and rough distance at all times, and you have advantage on checks to track or find it. Your attacks against your Favored Foe ignore all cover except Total Cover, and are unaffected by the Invisible condition or by magical concealment.

You gain the Land’s Stride feature if you do not have it. If you do, it improves: difficult terrain of any kind — natural, magical, or conjured — never costs you extra movement, and you leave no tracks unless you choose to. You gain a Climb Speed and Swim Speed equal to your Speed, and you can move across liquid, snow, and other unstable surfaces without sinking, provided you end your turn on solid ground. Additionally, you can use the Search action as a Bonus Action.
Your Second Wind now restores Hit Points equal to 2d10 + your Prestige Level. When you use Second Wind, you may also end one of the following conditions on yourself: Frightened, Poisoned, or Prone.

You gain the next tier of your Warden Specialization that your qualifying cycle hadn’t reached — and only that one. If your Ranger levels were below 9th, you gain Warden’s Covenant (9th). If your Ranger levels were 9th or higher, you gain Warden’s Pinnacle (14th) instead. You cannot switch to a different Warden Specialization with this feature

Whatever subclass you finished your qualifying cycle with stops there — it does not keep progressing on its own. The only way to unlock any further subclass tier is through this feature. Choose any Ranger archetype or any Fighter subclass — the one you already had, or a new one entirely. You gain its features at the matching Pathfinder Level: Ranger archetype: Pathfinder Level 3rd, 7th, 11th, and 15th. Fighter subclass: Pathfinder Level 3rd, 7th, 10th, 15th, and 18th.

At Pathfinder Level 4, 8, 12, 16, and 19, you can increase one ability score by 2, or two ability scores by 1, to a maximum of 20 (unless another feature allows otherwise). You may take a Feat instead.

When you take the Attack action, you can make one additional attack with the weapon you are wielding, provided at least one of the attacks in that action targets your Favored Foe. This is not an Extra Attack feature and does not interact with the rule against stacking them. It adds one attack to however many the Attack action already grants you, whether that is two or three.

You gain one additional use of Action Surge between rests. When you use Action Surge, you can also move up to your Speed without provoking Opportunity Attacks, and the first attack you make during the surged action against your Favored Foe is a Critical Hit on a roll of 18–20.

When a creature you can see within 60 feet moves, you can take a Reaction to move up to half your Speed toward it. If you end this movement within 30 feet of your Favored Foe, you may make one weapon attack against it as part of that Reaction. Additionally, you can follow your Favored Foe through teleportation or onto the Ethereal Plane — no other form of planar travel. When it teleports or shifts to the Ethereal Plane while you are within 60 feet, you may immediately follow, appearing in an unoccupied space within 10 feet of it. You can only return to the space you left (or the nearest unoccupied space to it) once your Favored Foe is dead, as a Bonus Action.

You gain the Evasion feature: when you make a Dexterity saving throw against an effect that deals half damage on a success, you instead take no damage on a success and half damage on a failure. Additionally, Opportunity Attacks against you are made with disadvantage.

Your Favored Foe’s defenses fail against you. Your attacks against it ignore Resistance to the damage type dealt, and reduce Immunity to Resistance. Your Favored Foe has disadvantage on saving throws against your Ranger spells and Pathfinder features. Additionally, your Primeval Awareness has no daily limit, and its range extends to 20 miles.

You have walked enough of the world that it answers to you. You are immune to Exhaustion from environmental sources and to extreme heat and cold, and you no longer need to eat or drink (you still require a Long Rest’s worth of rest). You may cast Commune with Nature, Find the Path, and Nondetection (self only) at will, without expending a spell slot or material components.

You gain the Indomitable feature with one use if you do not have it; if you do, you gain one additional use. When you use it, you may instead choose to automatically succeed on the saving throw if the effect came from your Favored Foe. Once you use that improvement, you can’t do so again until you finish a Long Rest.

Your Extra Attack feature lets you attack three times instead of twice when you take the Attack action. As normal, this does not stack with other features that set your number of Extra Attacks — if you already attack three times (from Fighter’s Extra Attack (2), for example), you instead add your Wisdom modifier to the damage of the final attack in the action. Hounding Strikes is separate and still adds its attack on top, putting every Pathfinder at four attacks by this level.

When you attack a creature that has not yet taken a turn in combat, or a creature that cannot see you, your attack roll cannot miss on anything other than a natural 1, and you deal an additional Trailblazer Die of damage on a hit.

Your years of experience sharpen into real mastery. Choose two skills you’re proficient in — you gain Expertise in both, doubling your proficiency bonus for ability checks using them. You also gain a third Fighting Style option (see Fighting Style) and one additional Weapon Mastery property choice.

You can spend 1 minute to open a path where none exists. You and up to twelve willing creatures travel to any location you have personally visited, or any location described to you in precise detail, arriving there after 1d4 hours. The journey passes through a shifting corridor of trails between places; you cannot be intercepted, tracked, or scried during the passage. Once you use this feature, you cannot use it again until you finish a Long Rest.
You have advantage on all attack rolls against your Favored Foe, and it has disadvantage on all attack rolls against you.

You are the first through the door and the last one standing in it. Foe Slayer. Add your Wisdom modifier to all damage rolls you make against your Favored Foe, weapon and spell alike. Nowhere Is Far Enough. Your Relentless Pursuit now lets you follow your Favored Foe through any form of planar travel, not just teleportation or the Ethereal Plane. The Next One. When your Favored Foe drops to 0 Hit Points, you can immediately designate a new creature and make one weapon attack against it, no action required. Once per turn. Last Standing. When you would be reduced to 0 Hit Points while your Favored Foe remains alive, you instead regain Hit Points equal to your Prestige Level and can immediately move up to your Speed towards your Favored Foe and make one attack against them. Once per Long Rest.

Description You master performance so that you can command any stage. You gain the following benefits: Increase your Charisma score by 1, to a maximum of 20. You gain proficiency in the Performance skill. If you are already proficient in the skill, you add double your proficiency bonus to checks you make with it. While performing, you can try to distract one humanoid you can see who can see and hear you. Make a Charisma(Performance) check contested by the humanoid’s Wisdom (Insight) check. If your check succeeds, you grab the humanoid’s attention enough that it makes Wisdom (Perception) and Intelligence (Investigation) checks with disadvantage until you stop performing.

The world we know has many rules and laws that dictate how it functions. Some explain why the sky is blue, others dictate how things fall, some even to help understand the best trajectory for a bolt or bullet. Regardless of what it may be, a Physicist is a specialized artificer that takes study of these natural laws to even greater lengths than most, learning to exploit them to achieve things previously thought impossible. While they may shy away from a technological side of artifice, make no mistake that the work of physicists is invaluable to almost all fields. Features 3rd Level - Analytic 3rd Level - Physicist Spells 3rd Level - Experimental Formulas 5th Level - Kinetic Bombard 9th Level - Advanced Formulas 15th Level - Newtonian Defiance
When you choose this specialization at 3rd level, you can add half your proficiency bonus (rounded down) to any Intelligence check you are not already proficient with.

You always have certain spells prepared after you reach particular levels in this class, as shown in the Physicist Spells table. These spells count as artificer spells for you, but they don’t count against the number of artificer spells you prepare.

3rd Level: Magnify Gravity, Magic Missile 5th Level: Borrowed Knowledge, Immovable Object 9th Level: Counterspell, Pulse Wave 13th Level: Gravity Sinkhole, Fire Shield 17th Level: Antilife Shell, Telekinesis

Starting at 3rd level, you learn various formulas that can be used to alter or improve your performance. You have a number of experiment points equal to half your artificer level (rounded down) and regain all expended points when you finish a long rest. Alternatively, you can expend a spell slot as an action to regain experiment points equal to the slot's level. You spend experiment points on different formulas, of which you learn three from the following list: Alternate Angle: When you make an attack with a weapon that deals bludgeoning, piercing, or slashing damage, you can expend one experiment point to change the damage type to a different type from the same list. The attack also deals an extra 3 damage. Thermodynamics: When you take fire or cold damage, you can use your reaction to expend one experiment point to deal half that damage of the opposite type to the creature that dealt the damage to you. Conservation of Energy: When you deal force damage to a creature or object, you can expend one experiment point to deal extra damage equal to half your artificer level. Doing so reduces your speed to 0 until the end of your next turn. Electron Shell: As an action, you can expend one to five experiment points to create a shell around you, which has 4 charges, plus one for every additional point spent. When you take damage, the damage is reduced by the amount of charges, and one is expended. All remaining charges dissipate after one hour. Polarize: When you make an attack or cast a spell that deals damage, you can expend an experiment point to forgo rolling damage to deal the average damage. Applied Science: When you make an ability check, you can expend an experiment point to predict the result before seeing it. If you are correct, you gain a +10 bonus to the roll. If you are within 1, you gain a +5 bonus instead.

Starting at 5th level, you are able to harness the outgoing kinetic energy of attacks. Once per round, when you make a weapon or spell attack, you can increase the damage of the attack by 2d4, this damage is force damage. The damage dealt by this ability increases to 3d4 at 9th level, and to 4d4 at 15th level.

A breakthrough has led to your creation of even further refined formulas. At 9th level you learn two of the following advanced formulas: Genius Precision: When you or a creature you can see within 30 ft of you make an attack roll, you can expend one experiment point to apply your flash of genius to the attack roll. Kinetic Battery: As a bonus action, you can expend one experiment point to begin storing kinetic energy. For every 10 feet you move, you add 1d6 to the total stored kinetic energy, up to 10d6. The next time you damage a creature or object, the target takes damage equal to your kinetic energy. The battery lasts for 1 minute, and if the battery expires before you deal damage, you take force damage equal to your kinetic energy. Meltdown: As an action, you can expend 2 experiment points to deal acid damage to a creature you can see within 60 ft equal to twice the amount of hit dice it has. This formula does not effect targets resistant or immune to acid damage. Super-Magnetism: If a spell or effect you create would move a creature on a failed saving throw, you can expend one experiment point to move the creature even if they succeed. You must use this formula before the creature makes the saving throw.

At 15th level, the natural laws of the world begin to bend at your command. You can cast the following spells with the following changes: Reverse Gravity: The spell has the normal effect, except that you can orient the area in any direction and creatures and objects fall toward the end of the area. Arcane Gate: The portals created by this spell can be oriented in any direction you choose, but must be created flat against a solid surface large enough to hold it. Telekinesis: You can manipulate up to three objects at once. If one of those objects is a weapon, you can attack with that weapon as if you were holding it. You can cast each of these spells once in this way, and must finish a long rest to do so again.

Facing a horde of demons, a lone warrior raises their blade high. With a single cleave, the demonic horde is silenced, their ranks having been cleft in two without mercy nor hesitation. Pursued by the local militia, a figure dressed in black, ragged attire performs an ancient technique. With a dagger whirling about, she spins in a perfect arc and vanishes into thin air, losing her hunters with ease. Facing down his mortal enemy, a martial practitioner displays the ultimate killing technique that he had spent his entire life perfecting, just for this moment. In exactly ten steps, he thrusts his blade with the force of the very heavens, impaling the man who had taken his family from him. These warriors go by many names; the ninjas of Kozakura, the daoists of Shou Lung, and even the henshin mystics of Tabot. Focused on practicing various martial forms to employ in battle, subterfuge, or survival, this archetype of combatant hailing from the east is most commonly referred to under one name— the practitioner.

The martial forms trained by practitioners are rooted very heavily to worldly practices. Unlike a monk’s training, which is focused on spiritualism and purifying the soul, these forms are tied to more earthly aspects. Many martial forms are passed down through generations, existing as deep-rooted tradition, and others are lost arts created by long-forgotten ancestors. These forms spread throughout regions, often going by different names with various cultural adjustments made depending on their respective uses.

For a practitioner, training in specific arts defines their existence. Whether it be making use of their ki, training their bodies to withstand the force of their forms, or perfecting the use of weaponry to their absolute peak, practitioners can eventually perform impossible feats and earth-shattering deeds.
