You have mastered the raw fundamentals of combat. Any feature in this class that refers to your level uses your Prestige Level (PL), which is calculated as L20 + Pugilist Level. Additionally, your Pugilist Save DC for all features is 8 + your Proficiency Bonus + \your choice of Strength or Constitution modifier.

Your years of fighting in back alleys and taverns have given you mastery over combat styles that use Unarmed Strikes and Pugilist weapons (Simple Melee weapons and Improvised weapons). You gain the following benefits while you are unarmed or wielding only Pugilist weapons, and not wielding a Shield: Bonus Unarmed Strike: You can make one Unarmed Strike as a Bonus Action. Fisticuffs Die: You can roll the die shown in the Fisticuffs column of the Pugilist Table in place of the normal damage of your Unarmed Strike or Pugilist weapons. Improved Improvisation: You have a talent for turning anything into a weapon. All improvised weapons and your unarmed strike gain your choice of the Sap or Topple mastery property for you.

You have Resistance to Bludgeoning damage, while have resistance to Bludgeoning damage from another source you instead have immunity to bludgeoning damage. Once your Prestige Level reaches 30, this hardiness expands to grant you resistance to Piercing and Slashing damage as well.

Your experiences beating the odds have given you a swagger you can channel in battle. This is represented by Moxie Points. You have a maximum number of Moxie Points as shown in the Pugilist Table. You regain all expended Moxie Points only when you finish a Long Rest. You can spend these points to fuel the following features: Brace Up: You can use a Bonus Action and expend 1 Moxie Point to brace for attacks. When you do so, roll your Fisticuffs die and gain a number of Temporary Hit Points equal to the number rolled plus your Prestige Level and your Constitution modifier. One-Two Punch: When you use your Bonus Action to make an Unarmed Strike, you can expend 1 Moxie Point to make two Unarmed Strikes as a Bonus Action instead of one. Stick and Move: You can use a Bonus Action and expend 1 Moxie Point to make one Unarmed Strike and take either the Dash or Disengage action.

When you take damage, you can use your Reaction to gain a surge of adrenaline. You gain Temporary Hit Points equal to six times your Pugilist Level. These Temporary Hit Points vanish if any remain when you finish a Short or Long Rest. Once you use this feature, you can’t use it again until you finish a Long Rest.

When you fail a Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, or Charisma check, you can expend 1 Moxie Point to attempt to swagger your way to success. Roll your Fisticuffs die and add the number rolled to the ability check, potentially turning it into a success. If the ability check still fails, you regain the expended Moxie Point.

You have learned to put your whole body into every strike. When you hit a creature with an Unarmed Strike, you can deal damage and use both your choice of the Grapple or Shove options against the target.
You can choose a pugilist archetype and you gain more features from the subclass on the following levels, PL26, PL31, PL37 Options: Dog and Hound Street Saint Squared Circle Piss and Vinegar

You can use a Bonus Action to find a hidden reserve of strength. For 1 minute, you have Resistance to Piercing and Slashing damage and you ignore the effects of Exhaustion levels 1 through 5. Once you use this feature, you can’t use it again until you finish a Long Rest unless you gain 1 level of Exhaustion (no action required) to restore your use of it.
Once per turn, when you make an attack with an Pugilist weapon or unarmed strike as part of your action you can make an additional unarmed strike as part of that same action

When you make an attack with an Unarmed Strike or Pugilist weapon, you can expend 3 Moxie Points to swing with wild abandon. On a hit, the attack becomes a Critical Hit. If the attack roll was already a Critical Hit, you instead triple the damage dice for the attack.

Whenever you deal damage with your Unarmed Strike or an attack with an improvised weapon, the strike is considered magical for the purpose of overcoming resistance and immunity to non-magical attacks, and you can choose to have it deal Force damage instead of its normal type.

While you are Bloodied (at or below half your maximum Hit Points), your spirit flares with desperation. You add a bonus to the damage of your Unarmed Strikes and Pugilist weapons equal to your Constitution modifier plus your current level of Exhaustion.

Once per turn, you can deal an extra 1d12 damage when you hit with an Unarmed Strike or Pugilist weapon. You can forgo this extra damage to apply one of the following effects: Endanger: The next time the creature is hit by an attack before the start of your next turn, the attack deals its maximum possible damage rather than rolling, this only applies to the pugilist or Unarmed strike damage, and not with any external damage riders Provoke: The creature has Disadvantage on attack rolls against creatures other than you until the end of your next turn.

Your physical prowess reaches legendary proportions. You gain the following benefits: Heavy Lifter: Your Strength score is doubled when determining your carrying capacity and the weight you can push, drag, or lift. Pillar Breaker: When you hit an object or structure with an Unarmed Strike, the hit is an automatic Critical Hit. Unmatched Athlete: Your jump distance is doubled.

At the start of each of your turns (no action required), you can expend 2 Moxie Points to remove one level of Exhaustion from yourself or end one of the following conditions on yourself: Blinded, Charmed, Deafened, Frightened, Paralyzed, Poisoned, Restrained, or Stunned.

Your resolve is bottomless. While your Dig Deep feature is active, you gain the following additional benefits: You can use your School of Hard Knocks feature twice per turn instead of once. You can attack three times, instead of twice, whenever you use one-two punch on your turn.

You have Advantage on Strength, Dexterity, and Constitution saving throws. Additionally, whenever you make a saving throw and fail, you can expend 1 Moxie Point to reroll it, and you must use the new roll.

When you roll Initiative, you can choose to remove one level of Exhaustion from yourself and regain your expended uses of Bloodied But Unbowed and Dig Deep. Once you use this feature, you cannot do so again until you finish a Long Rest. When you roll Initiative and have no uses of moxie left, you regain an amount equal to your Constitution Modifier.

When you are reduced to 0 Hit Points but not killed outright, you can drop to 1 Hit Point instead. When you do, you gain Temporary Hit Points equal to double your Prestige Level , and you have Resistance to all damage except Force for the next minute. While these Temporary Hit Points remain, you are immune to the Stunned and Paralyzed conditions. Once you use this feature, you can’t use it again until you finish a Long Rest.

You have reached the absolute zenith of mortal capability. You gain the following benefits: Hale and Hearty: You gain a permanent +2 to your AC while not wielding a shield and wearing only light armor or no armor, and your hit points increases by 40 Sleep It Off: When you finish a Long Rest, you lose all levels of Exhaustion rather than just one. Vim and Vigor: When you finish a Short Rest, you regain Hit Points equal to three times your Prestige Level.

Rough and wild looking, a human stalks alone through the shadows of trees, hunting the orcs he knows are planning a raid on a nearby farm. Clutching a shortsword in each hand, he becomes a whirlwind of steel, cutting down one enemy after another. After tumbling away from a cone of freezing air, an elf finds her feet and draws back her bow to loose an arrow at the white dragon. Shrugging off the wave of fear that emanates from the dragon like the cold of its breath, she sends one arrow after another to find the gaps between the dragon’s thick scales. Holding his hand high, a half-elf whistles to the hawk that circles high above him, calling the bird back to his side. Whispering instructions in Elvish, he points to the owlbear he’s been tracking and sends the hawk to distract the creature while he readies his bow. Far from the bustle of cities and towns, past the hedges that shelter the most distant farms from the terrors of the wild, amid the dense-packed trees of trackless forests and across wide and empty plains, rangers keep their unending watch.

Warriors of the wilderness, rangers specialize in hunting the monsters that threaten the edges of civilization—humanoid raiders, rampaging beasts and monstrosities, terrible giants, and deadly dragons. They learn to track their quarry as a predator does, moving stealthily through the wilds and hiding themselves in brush and rubble. Rangers focus their combat training on techniques that are particularly useful against their specific favored foes. Thanks to their familiarity with the wilds, rangers acquire the ability to cast spells that harness nature’s power, much as a druid does. Their spells, like their combat abilities, emphasize speed, stealth, and the hunt. A ranger’s talents and abilities are honed with deadly focus on the grim task of protecting the borderlands.

Though a ranger might make a living as a hunter, a guide, or a tracker, a ranger’s true calling is to defend the outskirts of civilization from the ravages of monsters that press in from the wild. In some places, rangers gather in secretive orders or join forces with druidic circles. Many rangers, though, are independent almost to a fault, knowing that, when a dragon or a band of orcs attacks, a ranger might be the first—and possibly the last—line of defense. This fierce independence makes rangers well suited to adventuring, since they are accustomed to life far from the comforts of a dry bed and a hot bath. Faced with city-bred adventurers who grouse and whine about the hardships of the wild, rangers respond with some mixture of amusement, frustration, and compassion. But they quickly learn that other adventurers who can carry their own weight in a fight against monstrous foes are worth any extra burden. Coddled city folk might not know how to feed themselves or find fresh water in the wild, but they make up for it in other ways.

As you create your ranger character, consider the nature of the training that gave you your particular capabilities. Did you train with a single mentor, wandering the wilds together until you mastered the ranger’s ways? Did you leave your apprenticeship, or was your mentor slain—perhaps by the same kind of monster that became your favored enemy? Or perhaps you learned your skills as part of a band of rangers affiliated with a druidic circle, trained in mystic paths as well as wilderness lore. You might be self-taught, a recluse who learned combat skills, tracking, and even a magical connection to nature through the necessity of surviving in the wilds. What’s the source of your particular hatred of a certain kind of enemy? Did a monster kill someone you loved or destroy your home village? Or did you see too much of the destruction these monsters cause and commit yourself to reining in their depredations? Is your adventuring career a continuation of your work in protecting the borderlands, or a significant change? What made you join up with a band of adventurers? Do you find it challenging to teach new allies the ways of the wild, or do you welcome the relief from solitude that they offer?

As a ranger, you gain the following class features Hit Points Hit Dice: 1d10 per ranger level Hit Points at 1st Level: 10 + your Constitution modifier Hit Points at Higher Levels: 1d10 (or 6) + your constitution modifier per ranger level after 1st Proficiencies Armor: Light, Medium, Shields Weapons: Simple and Martial Weapons Tools: Cartographer’s Tools, Herbalism Kit Saving Throws: Strength, Dexterity Skills: Choose three from Animal Handling, Athletics, Insight, Investigation, Nature, Perception, Stealth, and Survival

You have become adept at singling out enemies during combat, and may select one during each fight to increase your potency against. When you roll initiative, you may choose a creature that you can see to be designated as your Favored Foe, and you gain the following benefits: You gain a bonus to attack rolls against your Favored Foe equal to +2. Your Favored Foe always provokes opportunity attacks from you, even if they use an action or other special feature to prevent it. If your Favored Foe flees from combat, you have advantage on any check you make to locate it again If you already have a Favored Foe when you roll initiative, you can choose to keep it, without choosing a new one. Otherwise, you lose the benefits provided to you against your old Favored Foe.

You are particularly familiar with one type of environment and are adept at traveling and surviving in such regions. Choose one type of favored terrain: arctic, coast, desert, forest, grassland, mountain, swamp, or the Underdark. When you make an Intelligence or Wisdom check related to your favored terrain, your proficiency bonus is doubled if you are using a skill that you're proficient in. While traveling for an hour or more in your favored terrain, you gain the following benefits: Difficult terrain doesn't slow your group's travel. Your group can't become lost, except by magical means. Even when you are engaged in another activity while traveling (such as foraging, navigating, or tracking), you remain alert to danger. If you are travelling alone, you can move stealthily at a normal pace. When you forage, you find twice as much food as you normally would. While tracking other creatures, you also learn their exact number, their sizes, and how long ago they passed through the area. You choose additional favored terrain types at 6th and 10th level.

When you become a Ranger at 1st level, choose one of the following specializations to guide your playstyle. Iron Warden: You gain proficiency with Heavy Armor Earthen Warden: You can take the Hide action even if you are only lightly obscured. Nature’s Warden: You learn two cantrips of your choice from the Druid spell list.

At 2nd Level, you adopt a particular style of fighting as your specialty. CHoose one of the following options. You can’t take a Fighting Style option more than once, even if you later get to choose again. Archery: You gain a +2 bonus to attack rolls you make with ranged weapons. Blind Fighting: You have blindsight with a range of 10 feet. Within that range, you can effectively see anything that isn’t behind total cover, even if you’re blinded or in darkness. Moreover, you can see an invisible creature within that range, unless the creature successfully hides from you. Defense: While you are wearing armor, you gain a +1 bonus to AC. Dueling: When you are wielding a melee weapon in one hand and no other weapons, you gain a +2 bonus to damage rolls with that weapon. Thrown Weapon Fighting: You can draw a weapon that has the thrown property as part of the attack you make with the weapon. In addition, when you hit with a ranged attack using a thrown weapon, you gain a +2 bonus to the damage roll. Two-Weapon Fighting: When you engage in two-weapon fighting, you can add your ability modifier to the damage of the second attack.

By the time you reach 2nd level, you have learned to use the magical essence of nature to cast spells. See Spell Rules for general rules of spellcasting and the bottom of this document for the ranger spell list. Spell Slots: The Ranger table shows how many spell slots you have to cast your ranger spells of 1st level and higher. To cast one of these spells, you must expend a slot of the spell’s level or higher. You regain all expended spell slots when you finish a long rest. For example, if you know the 1st-level spell animal friendship and have a 1st-level and a 2nd-level spell slot available, you can cast animal friendship using either slot. Spells Known of 1st Level and Higher: You know two 1st-level spells of your choice from the ranger spell list. The Spells Known column of the Ranger table shows when you learn more ranger spells of your choice. Each of these spells must be of a level for which you have spell slots. For instance, when you reach 5th level in this class, you can learn one new spell of 1st or 2nd level. Additionally, when you gain a level in this class, you can choose one of the ranger spells you know and replace it with another spell from the ranger spell list, which also must be of a level for which you have spell slots. Spellcasting Ability: Wisdom is your spellcasting ability for your ranger spells, since your magic draws on your attunement to nature. You use your Wisdom whenever a spell refers to your spellcasting ability. In addition, you use your Wisdom modifier when setting the saving throw DC for a ranger spell you cast and when making an attack roll with one. Spell Save DC = 8 + your proficiency bonus + your Wisdom modifier Spell attack modifier = your proficiency bonus + your Wisdom Modifier
At 3rd level, you choose an archetype that you strive to emulate. Your choice grants you features at 3rd level, and again at 7th, 11th, and 15th level.

Additionally at 3rd level, you can open your mind to the presence of certain types of creatures. As an action, you may choose from aberrations, celestials, dragons, elementals, fey, fiends, and undead. For one minute, you know if any creatures of that type are within 5 miles of you, and the distance to the closest one. You can use this feature a number of times equal to your wisdom modifier before finishing a long rest.

When you reach 4th level, and again at 8th, 12th, 16th, and 19th level, you can increase one ability score of your choice by 2, or you can increase two ability scores of your choice by 1. As normal, you can’t increase an ability score above 20 using this feature. Using the optional feats rule, you can forgo taking this feature to take a feat of your choice instead.
Beginning at 5th level, you can attack twice, instead of once, when you take the attack action on your turn.

When you reach 6th level, your ability to hunt your quarry reaches new heights. Your ranged attacks ignore half cover, or three-quarters cover if the target is your Favored Foe. Additionally, your melee attacks against your Favored Foe cannot have disadvantage.

Starting at 8th level, you are no longer slowed by difficult terrain. Additionally, non-magical plants cannot slow your speed or harm you as you travel through them. You have advantage on any saving throw against plants that are magically created or manipulated to slow or damage you.

Your connection to your Warden specialization deepens when you reach 9th level, granting you further benefits based on your decision at 2nd level. Iron Warden: You gain a bonus to Strength (Athletics) and Dexterity (Acrobatics) checks equal to your wisdom modifier. Earthen Warden: You gain a bonus to Dexterity (Stealth) and Wisdom (Perception) checks equal to your wisdom modifier. Nature’s Warden: You gain a bonus to Intelligence (Arcana) and Intelligence (Nature) checks equal to your wisdom modifier.

Starting at 10th level, you gain a supernatural quickness while hunting your Favored Foe. While your Favored Foe lives, and you are in combat with it, your walking speed increases by 10 feet. Additionally, the bonus to attack rolls granted by your Favored Foe increases to be equal to your wisdom modifier (minimum bonus of +2)

When you reach 13th level, you gain the ability to magically conceal yourself. As a bonus action, you can cause yourself, and all equipment you are wearing or carrying, to turn invisible until the end of your next turn. You can use this feature a number of times equal to your proficiency bonus, and regain all expended uses when you finish a long rest.

At 14th level, the specialization you selected at 1st level grants you further benefits. Iron Warden: When you take the attack action on your turn, you can make three attacks, instead of two. Earthen Warden: You gain blindsight with a range of 60 feet, and tremorsense with a range of 30 feet. Nature’s Warden: You learn one spell from the druid spell list of 6th level of your choice. This spell counts as a ranger spell for you. You can cast this spell once without expending a spell slot, regaining the ability to do so when you finish a long rest.
At 18th level, you have advantage on all attack rolls made against your Favored Foe, and it has disadvantage on all attack rolls against you.
When you reach 20th level, being your Favored Foe is nothing short of a death sentence. Add your wisdom modifier to all damage rolls you make against your Favored Foe, weapon and spell alike.
Level 20 Cycle: You must have completed 20 levels of Ranger (X's Revised Again Ranger) with no multiclassing. Hit Dice: 1d10 per level

When you take this prestige class, choose two additional skills from the Ranger skill list. You gain proficiency in both.

You gain a new set of spell slots to fuel your spells. You gain spell slots as per the Ranger table based on your Prestige Level minus 20. Your number of spells known equals 11 plus the Spells Known entry on the Ranger table for your Prestige Level minus 20, as shown in the Spells Known column above. Because Ranger spellcasting begins at 2nd level, your new slots and spells begin at PL 22.
Your Warden Specialization reaches beyond mortal limits. You gain features based on your specialization at PL 21, 26, and 34, as detailed in the Warden's Ascension section below.

When you designate your Favored Foe, you learn its damage resistances, immunities, vulnerabilities, and condition immunities, plus its highest and lowest saving throws. Once per turn when you hit your Favored Foe with a weapon attack, you can change the damage type of that hit to acid, cold, fire, lightning, or poison.
Your talents expand. You may choose the same Ranger archetype, or a new one to broaden your craft. Your choice grants you features at PL 23, 27, 33, and 37.

At PL 24, 28, 32, 36, and 39, you can increase one ability score of your choice by 2, or two ability scores of your choice by 1. As normal, you can't increase an ability score above 20 using this feature. You may select a Feat instead.
When you reach 25th level your previous fighting styles grow to fit your new strengths. Any fighting style you gained through the ranger class or ranger archetype is improved in the following ways:
You have a +2 bonus to attack rolls with ranged weapons. Your ranged weapons also deal one additional damage die.
While you are wearing armor, you gain a +2 bonus to AC and saving throws.
You add your Wisdom modifier to the damage of any cantrip learned through Druidic Warrior.

When you are wielding a melee weapon in one hand and no other weapons, you gain a +2 bonus to damage rolls with that weapon. Additionally, creatures you hit with that weapon have disadvantage to hit anyone other than you until the start of your next turn.

When you roll a 1 or a 2 on a damage die for an attack roll you make with a melee weapon that you are wielding in two hands, you can reroll the damage die. You may reroll the damage die if the result is a 1 or a 2 as many times as you like. The weapon must have the two-handed or versatile property to gain this benefit.
When a creature you can see attacks a target other than you that is within 5 feet of you, you can use your reaction to cause that attack roll to automatically miss.
When you engage in two-weapon fighting, you can make one additional attack with the second weapon as part of the same bonus action, adding your ability modifier to both if it does not already.
The speed bonus from your Swift Hunter feature increases to 20 feet. Additionally, while your Favored Foe lives and you are in combat with it, you can take the Dash action as a Bonus Action.
When you have Advantage on an attack roll against your Favored Foe, you roll three d20s instead of two and use the highest result. This also applies to any check you make to locate your Favored Foe.

Your Primeval Awareness now has a range of 50 miles, and you can also choose beasts, giants, monstrosities, and plants. You learn the number of creatures of the chosen type and the direction to each one. While Primeval Awareness is active, you and allies within 30 feet of you can't be surprised by creatures of the chosen type, and you have Advantage on Initiative rolls.

When you hit your Favored Foe, it can't take Reactions until the start of your next turn, and its speed is reduced by 10 feet until then. This speed reduction can stack up to three times, reducing the speed by up to 30 feet.

When you use Nature's Veil, the invisibility lasts for 1 minute, or until you make two attack rolls or cast a spell. The number of times you can use Nature's Veil equals your Proficiency Bonus plus your Wisdom modifier.

You can make the Opportunity Attacks your Favored Foe provokes with a ranged weapon. The attack triggers when your Favored Foe leaves a space within 30 feet of you, or when it takes an action that would normally avoid provoking you. When you hit your Favored Foe with an Opportunity Attack, its speed becomes 0 until the end of its turn.

Once per round, you can make the Opportunity Attack your Favored Foe provokes without using your Reaction. Additionally, once per round when your Favored Foe misses you with an attack roll, you can make one weapon attack against it (no action required).

Your Foe Slayer feature now adds twice your Wisdom modifier to damage rolls against your Favored Foe. When you reduce your Favored Foe to 0 hit points, you regain hit points equal to your Prestige Level and one use of Nature's Veil. Additionally, your Wisdom score increases by 4, to a maximum of 30.

PL 21: Ironclad. While you are wearing Heavy Armor, the bludgeoning, piercing, and slashing damage you take is reduced by your Wisdom modifier. You also have Advantage on saving throws against being knocked Prone or moved against your will. PL 26: Unyielding Ward. When a creature within 5 feet of you makes an attack against a target other than you, you can use your Reaction to make one weapon attack against it. On a hit, the triggering attack has Disadvantage. PL 34: Mountain's Endurance. While you are wearing Heavy Armor, you have Resistance to bludgeoning, piercing, and slashing damage. Additionally, when you are reduced to 0 hit points but not killed outright, you drop to 1 hit point instead. Once you use this benefit, you can't do so again until you finish a Long Rest.

PL 21: Stone Shadow. You can take the Hide action as a Bonus Action. If you miss with an attack while hidden, you remain hidden. PL 26: Earthmeld. You gain a burrow speed equal to your walking speed. You can move through nonmagical earth and stone without disturbing the material you move through, and your tremorsense increases to 60 feet. PL 34: Unseen Predator. Your blindsight increases to 120 feet. Once per turn, when you hit a creature while hidden, you remain hidden if you are not within 5 feet of it.

PL 21: Primal Channel. You learn two additional cantrips from the Druid spell list. Additionally, when you learn a spell from Ascendant Spellcasting, you can choose it from the Druid spell list, and it counts as a Ranger spell for you. When you take the Attack action on your turn, you can replace one of the attacks with casting a druid cantrip you know. PL 26: Verdant Arcana. You learn one 7th-level spell from the Druid spell list. This spell counts as a Ranger spell for you. You can cast it once without expending a spell slot, regaining the ability to do so when you finish a Long Rest. PL 34: Heart of the Wild. You learn one 8th-level spell from the Druid spell list under the same terms as Verdant Arcana. Additionally, you regain the use of the 6th-level spell from your Warden's Pinnacle when you finish a Short Rest.

Decisive tactics and thoughtful planning are both highly important factors in the game of chess, and as certain Bulwarks are aware, the same goes for the art of war. Rooks are master tacticians, able to turn the tide of battle in their favor from nearly any position. Features: 3rd Level - One Step Ahead 7th Level - Recapture 13th Level - Gambits 18th Level - Checkmate

When you select this specialization at 3rd level, you learn to apply yourself on the battlefield in a similar way to the pieces of a chess board. You gain a pool of material equal to thrice your bulwark level to spend on plays. If a play allows you to move as part of it, you do so without expending your own movement, but you cannot have a speed of 0. You recover all expended material when you finish a long rest. Below is the list of plays: Advance: When you take the attack action, you may expend three material to move up to your speed. You may take this movement before or after you make your attacks. Back Rank: When you enter your defensive stance you can expend 3 material to impose disadvantage on all ranged attacks against you for the duration. En Passant: When you attack a creature within 5 feet of you, you may expend 2 material to move up to 10 feet to another point within 5 feet of that creature. This movement does not provoke opportunity attacks, and your next attack roll against it has advantage. Pawn’s Fury: During the first round of combat, you may expend 3 material to take an additional action. That action can be used to take only the Attack (one attack only), Dash, Disengage, Hide, or Interact with an Object action. Knight’s Leap: When you jump, you may expend 1 material to triple your jump distance. It does not cost you any additional movement to do so. Bishop’s Grace: As an action, you may expend 2 material to cast both guidance and resistance on yourself. Neither spell requires your concentration.
Starting at 7th level, you learn to reclaim the potential of the foes you fell. When you kill a creature with at least 30 hit points, you recover 5 material.

When you reach 13th level, you gain the ability to perform greater plays with great risk, though the potential payout is just as grand. You gain access to the following plays: Castling: When you enter your defensive stance, you may spend 7 material to choose one willing creature within 30 feet of you to trade places with. This movement does not provoke opportunity attacks. If when initiative ends, that creature has not taken damage since the switch, you regain 7 material. Discovered Attack: When a creature within 5 feet of you targets you with an attack, you may use your reaction to expend 10 material. In doing so, you may make a melee attack against that target. If the attack reduces the creature to 0 hit points, you regain 10 material. Promote: When you roll initiative, you may spend 20 material. For the duration of that combat you make plays, but not gambits, without expending material. Queen’s Majesty: As a bonus action, you may expend 25 material in order to move up to twice your speed. For one minute after taking this bonus action, the amount of material you gain from your recapture feature is doubled. King’s Command: As an action, you may spend 20 material to cast the Command spell (DC 8 + your strength modifier + your proficiency bonus) on any number of creatures within range. You must use the same command on each target. If no target succeeds their saving throw, you regain 10 material. Rook’s Defiance: When you use your Fortitude feature, you may spend up to 20 material and further reduce the damage by that amount. If you reduce the damage to 0, you regain half the material spent.

At 18th level, you have mastered the art of bringing fights to a decisive finish. When you take the attack action while your stance is active, you may choose to end your stance early. If you do, the first creature you hit takes extra damage equal to your bulwark level and is knocked prone.

Alone in a cave sits a near withered old human. Having spent decades honing his very mind, he finally stands. And the very land quakes as he does. A traveling monk spends years visiting temples across the world in an attempt to understand the nature of the very gods themselves. In doing so, a divine presence has rubbed off on them. A ridiculed gnome stomps out of a mages college, kicked out on the grounds of being unteachable. Unknown to both the gnome and the college, the abstract and unpredictable are a conduit of power themselves. A sage carries a deep understanding of arcane secrets, as well as knowledge of how magic truly works in regards to their spells and lives. Different ways of thinking are the true distinctions between sages, as no two have the exact same experiences or conclusions to their magical capabilities, even those who might have studied together. A sage draws on their understanding and connection to magic to call forth spells of great power.

Sages do not tend to study upon actual arcane knowledge, much like a wizard might. Instead using what they already know, and using that to expand upon their capabilities. The only true limiting factor of a sage is their own minds. As such, the ways a sage reflects upon their magic can greatly influence how it is formed and projected. Very rarely does a sage know from the beginning how their magic will take shape as they allow it to grow.

When creating a sage, knowing how your character perceives the world around them is crucial to both their development and their philosophies that shape their magic. Is your sage a hard working arcanist? Or perhaps more laid back? Your decisions should reflect your character's abilities and spells in how they are projected and used.

As a Sage, you gain the following class features.
Hit Dice: 1d6 per sage level. Hit Points at 1st Level: 6 + your constitution modifier Hit Points at Higher Levels: 1d6 (or 4) + your constitution modifier per Sage level after first.

Armor: none Weapons: Daggers, darts, slings, quarterstaffs, light crossbows Tools: none Saving Throws: Intelligence, Wisdom Skills: Choose two from Arcana, History, Insight, Medicine, Nature, Perception, Religion, Survival

You start with the following equipment, in addition to the equipment granted by your background: (a) a quarterstaff or (b) two daggers A component pouch (a) a scholar’s pack or (b) an explorer’s back (a) a light crossbow and 20 bolts or (b) a sling and 20 bullets

A deep connection to the weave and your surroundings allow you to tap into and utilize magic. Cantrips​ At first level, you know two cantrips of your choice from the Sage spell list. You learn additional Sage cantrips of your choice at higher levels, as shown in the Cantrips Known column of the Sage table. Spell Slots​ The Sage table shows how many slots you have to cast your sage spells of 1st level or higher. To cast one of these sage spells, you must expend a slot of the spell’s level or higher. You regain all expended spell slots when you finish a long rest. Spells Known of 1st Level and Higher​ You know two 1st-level spells of your choice from the sage spell list. The Spells Known column of the Sage table shows you when you learn more sage spells of your choice. Each of these spells must be of a level for which you have spell slots. For instance, when you reach 3rd level in this class, you can learn one new spell of 1st or 2nd level. Spellcasting Ability​ Wisdom is your spellcasting ability for your sage spells, since your magic relies on a deep understanding and connection to the weave. You use your Wisdom whenever a spell refers to your spellcasting ability. In addition, you use your Wisdom modifier when setting the saving throw DC for a sage spell you cast and when making an attack roll with one. Spell save DC = 8 + your proficiency bonus + your Wisdom modifier Spell Attack Modifier = your proficiency bonus + your Wisdom modifier Spellcasting Focus​ A Sage cannot use a spellcasting focus for their sage spells, as they require a direct path to the source of their magic without interruption. A Sage must provide any material components their spells call for. Magical spellcasting foci do not provide benefits to sage spells.

You can spend a time in meditation to reflect and relearn what magic you have learned. When you finish a short rest, you can replace one sage spell you know for another. The new spell you learn must be of a level for which you have spell slots. Additionally, once per long rest, when you replace a spell with this feature, you regain one expended spell slot of a level equal to the new spell or lower, but not higher than 5th level.

When you reach 2nd level, you choose a philosophical study that guides the way you project your magic. Philosophy of Diligence Philosophy of Fallacy Philosophy of Finality Philosophy of Mysticism Philosophy of Patience Philosophy of Evolution Your choice grants you features at 2nd level and again at 6th, 10th, 14th, and 18th level.

At 3rd level, you gain an increased ability to weave together both your own thoughts and the magic you cast. When you use your [Meditation] feature and learn a new spell, you can choose to make the new spell into your focused spell. When you finish a long rest, you can replace any of your focused spells with another spell of 1st level or higher that you know. You can have a number of focused spells as designated by the Focused Spells column of the Sage Table. When you focus on a spell, choose two of the following shapes to place on the spell. You can only have any given shape on one focused spell at a time. A mind shape’s effects apply only to the focused spell they are attached to, unless otherwise stated. Clarity​ The spell ignores material components, except for those consumed by the spell Cruel​ When a creature takes damage from the spell, it has disadvantage on ability checks until the end of its next turn. Ethereal​ The spell’s effects can travel through solid objects, and can target creatures and objects behind total cover. If a spell specifies you must see your target, you still must meet this requirement. Flowing​ You can change the casting time from one action to one bonus action. Focused​ You can treat your wisdom modifier as being 50% higher for the purposes of setting your spell save DC, your spell attack modifier, and for making any checks relating to the spell for the spell’s duration. Growing​ While you maintain concentration on the spell, you gain a +1 bonus to damage rolls for each round you do so. This bonus can be no greater than half your sage level. Guiding​ A creature targeted by the spell has advantage on ability checks until the end of its next turn. Prepared​ When you cast the spell, your proficiency bonus increases by 1 until the start of your next turn. This mind shape does not exclusively affect this focused spell. Shared​ If the spell has a range of self, you can cast it targeting a willing creature within 30 feet of you. Siphoning​ When you target a creature with the spell, you gain temporary hit points equal to the spell’s level.

When you reach 4th level, and again at 8th, 12th, 16th, and 19th level, you can increase one ability score of your choice by 2, or you can increase two ability scores of your choice by 1. As normal, you can’t increase an ability score above 20 using this feature. Using the optional feats rule, you can forgo taking this feature to take a feat of your choice instead.

At 10th level, you can perfectly clear your mind during meditation. When you replace a spell with your [Meditation] Feature, you can replace a number of spells equal to your wisdom modifier. You still gain only a single spell slot from meditation.

As high level magic is used for your spells, an amount flows back to you to fill the void it left behind. When you reach 17th level, casting a spell of 6th level or higher will replenish an expended spell slot of a level equal to half the level of the spell you cast (rounded up). You can use this feature a number of times equal to your proficiency bonus, regaining all uses when you complete a long rest.

At 20th level, your mind transcends your own body, sustaining you by mere thought alone. You no longer need to eat, drink, or sleep, and you are immune to the charmed and frightened conditions. Additionally, you gain one additional reaction per round, that can only be used to cast a spell that has a casting time of one reaction.

A sage who focuses on refining their own mind to fully control the magic they wield. Such arcanists hold themselves to particularly high degrees of perfection, allowing little room for failure even among the most basic of tasks. Their work in achieving this perfection however is reflected in full by their arcane mastery.
Meticulous work has gone into perfecting your spellcasting. When you cast a spell of 1st level or higher that deals damage, you may treat a roll of 1 on any damage die as a 2.
Through your constant work, your mental fortitude is nigh unbreakable. At 6th level, you gain proficiency in Charisma saving throws.

At 10th level, you can further shape your spells to reflect your diligence. When you cast a focused spell, it ignores a target’s resistance to damage. You also gain the following Mind Shape, which can be placed on your focused spells as normal:
When you roll damage with the spell, you can treat a dice roll of one below its maximum amount as its maximum amount.

At 14th level, control over your spells has given you a large degree of control over their success. When you cast a spell that requires you to make a check using your spellcasting ability, you can treat any d20 roll of 9 or lower as a 10. Additionally, your Quality Spellcasting feature now treats a roll of 1 or 2 on any damage die as a 3.

At 18th level, your mastery over your very mind has granted you the power to exert your will on others to a greater, and invariable effect. When a creature succeeds on a saving throw against one of your focused spells, you can choose to make them fail instead. Alternatively, if you miss on an attack roll with a focused spell, you can cause the attack to hit instead. Once you use this feature, you cannot do so again until you finish a long rest.

Sages who follow this philosophy, often called “Blue Mages” due to the color of the robes many traditionally wear, embody the ever-flowing state of the world and others, taking that change into themselves and granting them the uncanny ability to adapt their very beings into something that can at times be completely unrecognizable. Class features: 2nd Level - Bonus Proficiencies 2nd Level - Azure Lores 6th Level - Flesh Writer 10th Level - Shaper of Evolution 14th Level - Hardened Study 18th Level - Ever-Evolving

When you select this study at 2nd level, you gain proficiency with longswords and scimitars, as well as the survival and nature skills. Your proficiency bonus is doubled for any check you make that uses either of those skills.

Additionally at 2nd level, you begin to uncover the ability to fundamentally change yourself in order to accommodate your continually evolving magic, starting with the ability to take the abilities of the monsters you face, using them as your own. When you are targeted by a creature’s ability that does not originate from a weapon attack, spell, legendary action, or lair action, you can attempt to tap into a deeper understanding of it, and combine it with yourself. If you do so, any attack roll that is part of the ability automatically hits you, and any saving throw is automatically failed. Immediately after the effects are resolved, you may make a wisdom saving throw (DC 8 + the creature’s proficiency bonus + the creature’s constitution modifier). On a success, you may add the ability to your collection of Azure Lore, unless the creature’s challenge rating is higher than your sage level. You may only learn one Azure Lore ability per individual creature. Whenever you use your Meditation feature to replace a spell that you know, you may replace it with one of your Azure Lore abilities. You can cast the ability as a spell, expending a spell slot of a level determined by the challenge rating of the creature. You automatically have any cantrip-level ability you gain through this feature available when you learn it. Follow Link to view Table Challenge Rating Spell Slot Level < 1 Cantrip 1 - 3 1st 4 - 5 2nd 6 - 7 3rd 8 - 9 4th 10 - 11 5th 12 - 13 6th 14 - 15 7th 16 - 17 8th 18 - 20 9th Casting the spell requires Somatic components, but not Verbal or Material, and has a casting time equal to the action it took the original creature. If the ability has a recharge condition, you must meet that condition before you are able to cast that Azure Lore ability again. You may place mind shapes on your Azure Lore abilities as normal when you gain that feature at 3rd Level.

When you reach 6th level, you unlock the ability to tap into the abilities of the fallen and dead creatures you encounter. You may spend ten minutes while in contact with the corpse of a creature to attempt to absorb one of the abilities that it had in life. After the ritual has been completed, make a wisdom saving throw (DC 12 + the creature’s proficiency bonus + the creature’s constitution modifier). On a success, you may choose a single special trait from the creature to add to yourself. On a success or failure, you cannot use that corpse again to gain abilities through this feature. The added trait cannot be Legendary Resistance or Limited Magic Immunity. Once you add a trait to yourself, it cannot be removed by any means short of giving up the knowledge of the trait, which you can do as an action. You can maintain a number of these traits equal to your wisdom modifier. If you try to assimilate more traits than your maximum would allow, you may choose to give up one of your current traits for the new one.

At 10th level, your spells shift to better reflect the evolution that you yourself have undergone. When you cast any of your Azure Lore skills as Focused Spells, you may expend one spell slot level lower than you normally would need to (minimum of 1st level). You also gain the following Mind Shape, which can be placed on your focused spells as normal: Evolving: You can cast this spell as a reaction to a creature you can see within 60 feet of you ending their turn.

When you reach 14th level, you no longer need to completely lower your defenses in order to intertwine your understanding of the abilities of others. When you attempt to learn an Azure Lore ability, attack rolls no longer automatically hit you, and you no longer automatically fail saving throws.

Normal physical limits no longer apply to the abilities you learn from your Azure Lore feature when you reach 18th level. You are now able to copy natural weapons, and Legendary Actions that target you. If you cast a creature’s Legendary Action as a spell, it takes an action to do so.

There are ways of thinking that are often called incorrect by many, exhibiting illogical methods, or even simply being incorrect. However, certain Sages can utilize these ways of thinking in shaping their magic into something truly bizarre.

The spells you cast carry the capacity to trick the very weave itself into allowing extra magic to be cast. When you cast a focused spell by expending a spell slot of first level or higher, the next time you or a creature within 30 feet of you casts that same spell at the same level before the start of your next turn, they do so without expending a spell slot, so long as the spell is of 5th level or lower.

Your illogical reasoning extends far enough to prevent harm to you, though opening you to potentially greater damage. Starting at 6th level, as a reaction when you take damage, you can teleport to an unoccupied space you can see within 30 feet of you, creating an illusory copy to take the damage instead. If you take damage from any source before the start of your next turn, you are vulnerable to that damage.

At 10th level, you can further shape your spells to your own fallacy. When a creature casts one of your focused spells that benefits from your [Bandwagon] feature, that creature gets advantage on the next attack roll, ability check, or saving throw they make within the next minute. You also gain the following Mind Shape, which can be placed on your focused spells as normal:
When you cast the spell, you can choose to have it not take effect until you cast your next spell.

You learn to use your thoughts to distract those around you at 14th level. When a creature within 60 feet of you makes an attack roll, ability check, or saving throw, you can use your reaction to impose disadvantage on the roll. If the creature fails their ability check, saving throw, or attack roll, it takes psychic damage equal to half your sage level. If it succeeds, you take the damage instead. You can do so a number of times equal to your Wisdom modifier, regaining all uses after you finish a long rest.

At 18th level, you gain the ability to turn other’s perceptions to better serve your spellcasting, and at a heavy detriment to them. As an action, you can force a creature within 60 feet of you to make a charisma saving throw against your spell save DC. On a failed save, the creature will willingly fail any saving throw against your sage spells, and is no longer considered willing for beneficial effects from allies. This effect lasts for 1 minute. Once you use this feature, you cannot do so again until you finish a long rest.

Those who undertake the Philosophy of Finality hold the understanding that all things must come to their eventual end. Inclusive of their foes, and themselves. A Sage who follows this study may work to bring, delay, or even stop the meddling with of such events. Regardless of how these Sage’s may work, they have a full understanding that it cannot, and will not last forever.

As your pool of magic runs out, you manage to extort additional power drawing from its end. When you cast a spell of 1st level or higher, and expend the last spell slot of a given level, you gain a bonus to one damage roll equal to 2d8.

At 6th level, lasting harmful effects are far less effective against you, as your understanding forces them to end. When you are targeted by a harmful effect with a duration of one minute or longer, you can choose to end the effect at the end of your next turn (no action required). Once you do so, you cannot do so again until you complete a short or long rest.

At 10th level, your spells reflect the absolute finality that shapes your spells. When a focused spell ends on a creature, you can choose to end all beneficial or detrimental effects currently affecting them. You also gain the following Mind Shape, which can be placed on your focused spells as normal:

If the spell causes a creature to be reduced to 0 hit points, it does not consume a spell slot. Once your denying spell prevents a spell slot from being expended, it cannot do so again until you create a new denying spell.

Your understanding of the end of all around you can allow you to bring it to the present instantly, empowering you in the process. At 14th level, you learn the Dispel Magic spell if you don’t already know it. You cannot replace this spell through meditation, and it does not count towards the total number of spells you know. When you successfully end a spell or effect with Dispel Magic, you can use your Last Cast feature on the next spell you cast of 1st level or higher, even if you have spell slots remaining of the level you cast.

At 18th level, the knowledge of your end fuels you to persist should you fall before your time. If you die to any source other than old age, you are returned to life 24 hours later with all of your hit points at the location you died, so long as your soul is able to. If your body was destroyed, a new one is created. Once you are restored to life by this feature, you cannot do so again until you finish a long rest.

There are those who take their connection to magic to a completely higher level, sometimes utilizing understanding through godly entities or beings of similar power. Sages who undertake the Philosophy of Mysticism may work closely with clerics, paladins, or even warlocks to further strengthen their connection to the divine.

When you take this philosophy at 2nd level, you gain a small spark connecting you to a divine entity, granting you enhanced magic. Choose two spells of 1st level from the Cleric or Warlock spell lists. Both spells need not be from the same list. These spells count as sage spells for you, and do not count towards your number of spells learned. If you choose to replace either of these spells through Meditation[1], you can learn a Cleric or Warlock spell of any level of which you have spell slots to cast in its place.

Your spells carry with them the capacity to heal both yourself and your allies. At 6th level, when you cast a sage spell of 1st level or higher that targets either you or an ally, you can cause that creature to restore a number of hit points equal to your sage level. You can do so a number of times equal to your wisdom modifier, and regain all expended uses when you finish a long rest.

At 10th level, you can further shape your spells to more closely fit the divinity you follow. When you cast a focused spell from the cleric or warlock spell lists, you can choose to have the spell count as one level higher than the slot used to cast it. In doing so, you can cast no spells other than focused spells for the next minute. You also gain the following Mind Shape[1], which can be placed on your focused spells as normal:
When a celestial, fiend, or undead fails a saving throw against the spell, or are hit with a spell attack roll, they take extra damage equal to half your sage level.

Your mental connections to divine magic have had a profound effect on both your mind and body at 14th level. When you make a charisma check, you can add your wisdom modifier to the total. Additionally, angel or bat wings sprout from your back (your choice) giving you a flying speed of 30 ft. You also gain resistance to radiant damage (if you chose angel wings), or necrotic damage (if you chose bat wings).

At 18th level, your spells carry with them the very essence of the divine entities you’ve spent your life connected with. You gain the following benefits. You can replace the damage type of your focused spells with radiant or necrotic. Celestials, Fiends and Undead have disadvantage on saving throws against your sage spells. When you restore hit points of another creature with a sage spell, you regain hit points equal to half the amount you healed. ↑ 1.0 1.1 Sage

So it is said that with patience comes wisdom. That wisdom can come in the form of great magical power for those who take upon patience into their very being. A sage who has undertaken the philosophy of patience is never the first to start conflict, but is rarely the first to fall as a result of it.
A sage of patience is always prepared should theirs outweigh that of others. As such, you gain proficiency in light armor, medium armor, and shields.

Starting at 2nd level, you gain the ability to enhance your longer lasting spells at the cost of a slower start. When you cast a spell that makes multiple damage rolls, or lasts for multiple rounds, the first damage roll, or damage rolls during the first round, have all damage dice treated as their lowest value. In return, the last damage roll, or damage rolls during the final round, have all damage dice treated as their highest amount.

Your spells open a window of clarity to you, allowing you to avoid harm for a short time immediately after casting them. Starting at 6th level, you can take the dodge action as a bonus action if you use your action to cast a sage spell of 1st level or higher.

At 10th level, your spells further evolve to reflect your patience. When you cast a focused spell, you gain temporary hit-points equal to your sage level. You also gain the following Mind Shape, which can be placed on your focused spells as normal:
Creatures cannot react to you casting this spell.

While concentrating on spells, both your mind and body become far more rigid. Starting at 14th level, while you maintain concentration on a spell, you gain a +2 bonus to your armor class and saving throws. Your concentration also cannot be broken as a result of taking damage.

At 18th level your patience opens opportunities to you that others could not even hope to achieve. When you roll initiative, you may choose to instead place yourself at initiative 0. If you do so, you may take a second turn immediately after your first turn in the first round of combat.

Sometimes seen as the oddball of the various Artificer specialists, the Scrapper is a master of what other Artificers discard as junk. Make no mistake though, these hoarder misfits exemplify everything an artificer is at their core - Innovative, curious, with a spark of insanity mixed in with genius. They take what others see as trash, and turn it into works of art. Features: 3rd Level - Tool of the Trade 3rd Level - Scrapper Spells 3rd Level - Another's Treasure 5th Level - Extra Attack 9th Level - Junkrat's Armor 15th Level - Sage of Junk

You have proficiency with improvised weapons. You also gain proficiency with smith's tools. If you already have this proficiency, you gain proficiency with one other type of artisan's tools of your choice.

Starting at 3rd level, you always have certain spells prepared after you reach particular levels in this class, as shown in the Scrapper Spells table. These spells count as artificer spells for you, but they don’t count against the number of artificer spells you prepare. 3rd level - magic missile, shield 5th level - cloud of daggers, locate object 9th level - leomund's tiny hut, melf's minute meteors 13th level - dimension door, fire shield 17th level - passwall, steel wind strike

Beginning at 3rd level, you can take anything lying around - A table leg, a shard of glass, a cooking pot - and turn it into a deadly weapon of war. When you hold/make an improvised weapon, the DM will determine if it deals slashing, piercing, or bludgeoning damage, and if it is one-handed (base 1d4 damage) or two-handed (base 1d6 damage) based on its resemblance to real weapons. You can use a bonus action to use your smithing tools to roll on the Upgrade Table to apply a random upgrade to an improvised weapon you are holding. An upgraded improvised weapon count as magical for the purpose of overcoming resistance and immunity to nonmagical attacks and damage. d6 - Effect 1 Heavy Smashers. You affix heavy weights to the weapon, adding a bonus 1d6 bludgeoning damage. When you damage a target with this weapon, roll 1d4. On a 4, you can knock the target away from you up to 10 feet. 2 Spiky Stabbers. You attach spiky things such as rusted nails, sharpened sticks, etc. to your weapon, adding a bonus 1d6 piercing damage. When you damage a target with this weapon, roll 1d4. On a 4, you reduce that target's AC by 2 until the end of its next turn. 3 Sharp Slicers. You add sharp metal scraps, broken glass, or other slicing edges to your weapon, adding a bonus 1d6 slashing damage. When you damage a target with this weapon, roll 1d4. On a 4, the target's speed is halved until the end of its next turn. 4 Burning Flames. You coat the weapon in flammable materials, and set it alight, adding a bonus 1d6 fire damage. When you damage a target with this weapon, roll 1d4. On a 4, you can ignite the target. A target on fire takes 1d10 fire damage at the start of its turn. The target can use an action to put the fire out. 5 Shocking Coils. You wrap your weapon with suspect electrical components and wires, adding a bonus 1d6 lightning damage. When you damage a target with this weapon, roll 1d4. On a 4, the target must succeed on a Constitution saving throw or be stunned until the end of its next turn. 6 Venomous Goo. You slather the weapon in dangerous chemicals and diseased meat, adding a bonus 1d6 poison damage. When you damage a target with this weapon, roll 1d4. On a 4, the target must succeed on a Constitution saving throw or become poisoned for 1 minute. The target can repeat the saving throw at the end of each of its turns, ending the effect on itself on a success. An upgraded improvised weapon can be used in a number of attacks equal to your Intelligence modifier plus your proficiency bonus(a minimum of twice) before they break and become unusable. You can apply only one upgrade on an improvised weapon and it is removed when you drop or stow the weapon. If you try to upgrade another improvised weapon, the old upgrade is immediately removed, and then the new upgrade applies. You can also consume a spell slot to apply an upgrade to an improvised weapon as a bonus action. If you do, you may choose the upgrade applied from the Upgrade Table. You are able to apply your infusions to your upgraded improvised weapons.
Starting 5th level, you can attack twice, rather than once, whenever you take the Attack action on your turn.

At 9th level, you have found new uses for all the scrap you carry around for makeshift weapons. Now, you know how to enhance your armor with ad hoc ablative shielding. After finishing a long rest and if you are wearing medium or heavy armor, your armor gains a bonus to Armor Class equal to your Intelligence modifier (a minimum bonus of +1). Whenever you take damage, roll 1d4. On a 4, pieces of this scrap-built extra armor break off, and your bonus decreases by 1 point until it returns to its normal base value.

By 15th level, you have become a lethal force with any random object that fits your fancy: Whenever you hold an improvised weapon, you can automatically apply a random upgrade from the Upgrade Table. When you cast a spell of 1st level or higher, the next attack you make with an upgraded improvised weapon deals extra force damage equal to 1d10 times the level of the spell cast, to a maximum of 5d10. You now gain the Junkrat's Armor bonus after a short or long rest, instead of only a long rest.

The practice of the Shinobi originates from the distant nation of Kozukura , a land historically isolated by treacherous mountains and seas. Unlike the mages of Faerûn who rely on external incantations and manipulation of the Weave , the people of Kozukura developed an intense internal discipline.

In Kozukura, the native population rarely developed an affinity for conventional spellcasting. Instead, they focused on channeling their Chakra—the energy formed by the perfect molding of their physical stamina and spiritual willpower. This internal manipulation allowed them to perform Jutsu (deadly techniques), achieving effects that mimic arcane magic without needing arcane components or external control. Shinobi techniques are, in essence, a hyper-focused method of drawing upon one's own life force to manipulate the ambient magical energy, providing results through sheer internal command.

Generations ago in Kozukura, genetic traits granting unique chakra abilities began to manifest in certain bloodlines. As the Kozukura culture did not prioritize traditional Weave magic, those with similar Bloodline abilities naturally flocked together and founded the great Clans (such as the Uchiha and Hyuga equivalents) to protect and enhance their technique. Over the centuries, economic necessity, trade, and occasional military conflict led to the gradual migration of Kozukura descendants across Faerûn. As this diaspora spread across the continent: Genetic Manifestation: The Bloodline abilities—such as the Copy Eye or Vitality—began manifesting randomly in individuals throughout the Sword Coast and beyond, regardless of their immediate family name. Hidden Centers: The most dedicated descendants established hidden villages or secluded Dojos across Faerûn. These centers remain vital for teaching the disciplines of chakra control and Jutsu mastery, ensuring that the Shinobi remains a rare and specialized operative utilizing unique tools and armor.

As a Shinobi, you gain the following class features.
Hit Dice: 1d8 per Shinobi level Hit Points at 1st Level: 8 + your Constitution modifier Hit Points at Higher Levels: 1d8 (or 5) + your Constitution modifier per Shinobi level after 1st

Armor: Light armor, medium armor Weapons: Simple weapons, shortswords, scimitars, hand crossbows, kusarigama Tools: Calligrapher's Supplies, Herbalism kit Saving Throws: Dexterity, Intelligence Skills: Choose three from Acrobatics, Athletics, Deception, History, Insight, Investigation, Perception, Sleight of Hand, and Stealth

You start with the following equipment, in addition to the equipment granted by your background: (a) a shortsword and 5 Kunai or (b) two simple weapons and 5 shuriken (a) a dungeoneer's pack or (b) an explorer's pack (a) leather armor or (b) chain Shirt (a) Calligrapher's Supplies and 10x tags (empty scrolls) (b) herbalism Kit

You have undergone rigorous conditioning in the arts of the silent kill and tactical movement. You gain the following benefits: Shinobi Weapons: You are a master of small, concealable arms. When you wield a kunai, kama, or shuriken, its damage die changes to a d6. These weapons, along with tanto, wakizashi and Kusarigama count as "Shinobi Weapons" for you, Shinobi Weapons are used when performing Bukijutsu. Kunai = Dagger Kama = Sickle Shuriken = Dart Tanto = Shortsword Wakizashi = Scimitar Ballistics: If a Shinobi Weapon has the Thrown property, its normal range increases to 30 feet and its long range increases to 90 feet. Armored Agility: Your conditioning allows you to move unrestricted. You can use your Dexterity score instead of Strength for calculating jumping distances and climbing checks, even while wearing Light or Medium armor.

Every Shinobi has an innate elemental affinity, determined by the alignment of their chakra at birth. Choose one of the following natures, alternatively roll a d8 to randomly select a nature. Random (D8) Nature Associated Element 1 Fire (Katon) Flame and Heat 2 Water (Suiton) Liquid and Ice 3 Earth (Doton) Soil and Stone 4 Wind (Futon) Air and Sound 5 Lightning (Raiton) Electricity 6 Yin (Genjutsu) Mind and Shadow 7 Yang Life and Vitality 8 Taijutsu & Bukijutsu Body and Force Primary Nature Efficiency: You are most efficient when molding chakra for your natural affinity. When you cast a Jutsu that matches the Primary Nature you selected at 1st Level, you reduce the Chakra cost by 1 (to a minimum of 1 Chakra). Primary Nature Technique: You learn a D Rank Jutsu of your Chosen Nature. This Jutsu doesn't count against the amount of Jutsu known

You have learned to mold your physical stamina and spiritual energy into Chakra, the fuel for your techniques. Chakra Points: You have a pool of Chakra points represented by the following formula: Chakra Maximum = Shinobi Level × 2 Recovery: You regain all expended Chakra points when you finish a Long Rest.

You have trained your memory and dexterity to weave Hand Signs, manifesting reality-warping effects known as Jutsu. Jutsu Known: You know a number of Jutsu equal to half your Shinobi level (rounded up) (minimum of 1). Learning New Jutsu: Whenever you gain a level in this class, you can replace one Jutsu you know with another Jutsu of a Rank you can cast. Jutsu Ranks: Jutsu are organized by Rank, which corresponds to their power level and Chakra cost. At 1st Level, you can learn and cast D-Rank Jutsu. You unlock higher ranks as you level up. Spellcasting Ability: Intelligence is your spellcasting ability for your Jutsu. Jutsu Save DC = 8 + your Proficiency Bonus + your Intelligence modifier Jutsu Attack Modifier = your Proficiency Bonus + your Intelligence modifier Jutsu Components: Hand Signs (Somatic Components): Casting a Jutsu requires you to weave complex hand signs. You must have two free hands to cast a Jutsu, unless a feature allows otherwise. You cannot cast Jutsu while holding a shield or a two-handed weapon, unless you drop it or put it away first. Material: These are varying components required when casting a jutsu Motion: Cannot perform with a speed of 0 Items: An Item that is required Gaze: Requires direct line of sight to the target Weapon: You must wield or have a weapon available to use a jutsu with a weapon component Jutsu and Magic: Jutsu count as spells, and casting a Jutsu counts as casting a spell, for the purpose of any effect that prevents, suppresses, or restricts spellcasting (such as an antimagic field or a raging Barbarian's restriction). Hand Signs count as Somatic components, so anything that prevents Somatic components also prevents Jutsu casting. Where an effect cares about spell level (such as Counterspell or Dispel Magic), a Jutsu's Rank counts as its Equivalent Spell Level from the Jutsu Rank & Cost Table (treat A-Rank as 5th level). Overcharging: Some Jutsu list an Overcharge option. When you cast such a Jutsu, you can spend additional Chakra on it, up to a maximum of additional Chakra equal to your Proficiency Bonus per casting. Extra damage dice gained from Overcharging always use the Jutsu's own damage die. Chakra cost reductions (such as Primary Nature Efficiency, Bloodline Efficiency, or Sannin Mode) apply only to a Jutsu's base cost, never to Overcharge Chakra. Standard Overcharge rates: +1 damage die costs 1 Chakra for a d4 or d6, 2 Chakra for a d8, or 3 Chakra for a d10; +1 target, projectile, or attack costs 2 Chakra; other effects (size, duration, wall HP, and so on) cost 2 Chakra per step. Basic Techniques: The basic utility technique of each nature (Basic Flame Control and the Basic Earth, Lightning, Water, Wind, Yin, and Yang Style Techniques) costs 1 Chakra to cast.
