Your capabilities are defined by your genetics or clan origin. Choose one Bloodline from the list below. This choice is permanent and cannot be changed. You automatically learn the Bloodline Jutsu associated with your chosen bloodline at the applicable Rank level. These do not count against your Jutsu Known. Bloodline Efficiency: When you cast one of your Bloodline Jutsu, reduce its Chakra cost by 1 (to a minimum of 1). Bloodline Jutsu have no elemental nature and do not benefit from Primary Nature Efficiency. Optional Rule: For Characters that do not know their genetic origin or who got the bloodline through far of generational mean, roll a d10 and divide it by 2 (rounded up) to determine your Bloodline Random Roll (1d10/2) Bloodline 1 The Copy Eye 2 The White Eye 3 The Whirlpool 4 The Shadow 5 The Prodigy

Descendants of a clan known for intense emotions and the Sharingan, an eye that sees chakra and mimics movement, when awakened the eye turns red with a single rain drop pattern. At each Bloodline level, you gain another raindrop. Kinetic Vision: You can briefly read the muscle tension of your enemies. When a creature you can see makes an attack roll against you, you can use your Reaction to impose Disadvantage on that attack roll. You can use this feature a number of times equal to your Proficiency Bonus, regaining all expended uses on a Long Rest.

Descendants of a noble clan possessing the Byakugan, capable of seeing long distances and through objects. Their eyes, pupils and irises are permanently white. All-Seeing: You cannot be Surprised while you are conscious.

Descendants of a fallen clan renowned for their sealing jutsu and immense longevity and larger than normal chakra pools. Massive Reserves: Starting at 2nd Level, you add your Proficiency Bonus to your Maximum Chakra Points.

Descendants of a clan of high-IQ tacticians who manipulate shadows to bind enemies. Shadow Arts: You learn the Minor Illusion cantrip. Intelligence is your spellcasting ability for it. You can cast it using only Somatic components (your shadow).

You possess no special surname, but you were born with a freakish talent for chakra manipulation Precision: When you roll damage for a Jutsu or a Shinobi Weapon attack, you can reroll any 1s on the damage dice. You must use the new roll.

At 3rd level, you choose the personal philosophy that guides your actions and techniques. Your choice grants you features at 3rd, 7th, 15th, and 20th Level. Nindo Efficiency: Once per Long Rest, when you use a Nindo feature (not a Jutsu) that requires you to spend Chakra, you can use it without spending Chakra. Nindo of the Iron Fist Nindo of the Battlemind Nindo of the Elementalist Nindo of the Illusionist Nindo of the Healer Nindo of the Assassin

When you reach 4th level, and again at 8th, 12th, 16th, and 19th level, you can increase one ability score of your choice by 2, or you can increase two ability scores of your choice by 1. As normal, you can't increase an ability score above 20 using this feature. Using the optional feats rule, you can forgo taking this feature to take a feat of your choice instead.
Beginning at 5th level, you can attack twice, instead of once, whenever you take the Attack action on your turn.

The latent power in your genetics begins to manifest more potent abilities. You gain the feature corresponding to the Bloodline you chose at 2nd Level. The Copy Eye Visual Insight: You can focus your chakra to see the unseen. You can cast See Invisibility or Detect Magic by spending 2 Chakra. You do not need material components for these castings. Reflexive Analysis: You gain proficiency in the Insight skill. If you are already proficient, you gain Expertise (doubling your proficiency bonus). The White Eye Piercing Sight: As a Bonus Action, you can activate your X-Ray vision for 1 minute. For the duration, you can see through solid objects to a range of 30 feet. Within that range, you have Blindsight. You can use this feature once per long rest, unless you spend 3 Chakra for each subsequent use. Reflexive Analysis: You gain proficiency in the Perception skill. If you are already proficient, you gain Expertise (doubling your proficiency bonus). The Whirlpool Vigorous Casting: Your chakra is so dense that it physically reinforces your body. Whenever you spend Chakra to cast a Jutsu of C-Rank or higher, you gain Temporary Hit Points equal to Your Constitution Modifier + The Jutsu's Chakra Cost. The Shadow Split Shadow: When you cast the Shadow Bind Jutsu, you can target two creatures instead of one, provided the targets are within 10 feet of each other. The chakra cost remains the same. The Prodigy Polymath: You gain Expertise in two skills of your choice in which you are proficient. Your proficiency bonus is doubled for any ability check you make that uses either of the chosen skills.

You have learned to center your breathing and stamina to recover quickly during downtime. Chakra Recovery: Once per day when you finish a Short Rest, you can meditate to regain expended Chakra equal to your Shinobi level. Centered Breathing: You have Advantage on Constitution saving throws made to maintain Concentration on a Jutsu.

Primary Nature: You gain more control over your Primary Nature and your jutsu becomes more powerful. You gain a +1 to any Jutsu attack rolls and +1 to the Save DC of any Jutsu you cast from your Primary Nature. Secondary Nature: You can choose any other Nature, or roll on the nature table (rerolling if you roll the same as your Primary) to be your Secondary, or secondary nature. You learn a D- Rank Jutsu from this nature, that does not count as one of your known jutsu

At 10th level, you master the art of focusing chakra into the soles of your feet to defy gravity and surface tension. You can move up, down, and across vertical surfaces and upside down along ceilings, as well as across liquids, without falling during the move. When you end your turn on a vertical surface, or upside down, you must spend 1 chakra to maintain the position or fall to the ground

At 11th level, your senses have become so attuned to the flow of chakra and the natural world that you can detect hidden threats and move unseen. You gain the following benefits: Chakra Sense: As an Action, you can open your mind to detect the presence of chakra for 1 minute. For the duration, you know the location of any creature within 60 feet of you that is not a Construct or Undead, even if the creature is hidden or invisible. You also detect the presence of magical objects or active spells/jutsu within the same range. You can use this feature a number of times equal to your Intelligence modifier (minimum of once), regaining all expended uses when you finish a Long Rest. Traceless Step: You leave no physical tracks, and you cannot be tracked by non-magical means unless you choose to leave a trail. Silent Signaling: You can communicate simple ideas (such as "Stop," "Enemy Ahead," "Go," or "Help") to your allies using only hand signs and body language. Allies who can see you understand these signals automatically; other creatures must make an Insight check (DC equal to your Jutsu Save DC) to decipher them.

Your genetic abilities have reached their mature state. You gain the feature corresponding to the Bloodline you chose at 2nd Level. The Copy Eye Susanoo Ribcage: You can manifest a spectral avatar of chakra to protect you from harm.When you take damage, you can use your Reaction and spend 4 Chakra to reduce the damage by 4d10 + your Intelligence modifier. If the damage is reduced to 0, you suffer no secondary effects from the attack (such as being pushed or poisoned). The White Eye Tenketsu Needle (Chakra Blocking): You can inject chakra into an opponent's pressure points to shut down their body. When you hit a creature with an Unarmed Strike or a Shinobi Weapon, you can spend 3 Chakra to force the target to make a Constitution saving throw. On a failed save, the target is Stunned until the end of your next turn. Additionally, whether they save or fail, they cannot take Reactions until the start of your next turn. The Whirlpool Hereditary Fortitude: You gain a bonus to your maximum hitpoint equal to the size of your Chakra pool The Shadow Shadow Strangle: You can crush the life out of those caught in your trap. As a Bonus Action, you can constrict the shadows around any creature currently Restrained by any of your bloodline jutsu. The target takes Necrotic damage equal to 3d8 + your Intelligence modifier. This damage does not break the hold or grant a new saving throw. The Prodigy Perfect Recall: Your understanding of chakra theory is absolute. You can cast a Jutsu from the Shinobi class list that you do not know. To do so, you must spend the standard Chakra cost of the Jutsu plus 2 additional Chakra. (e.g., Casting an unknown C-Rank Jutsu costs 3 + 2 = 5 Chakra). Mental Fortitude: You gain proficiency in Wisdom saving throws.

Primary Nature: The Bonus to your Jutsu Attack rolls and saving DC increases to 2 for All Jutsu tied to your Primary nature. Secondary Nature: You add a +1 to your jutsu attack rolls and Save DC for your Secondary Nature

At 18th level, your experience and efficiency in combat are second to none. You have mastered the art of weaving signs with minimal movement and blistering speed. One-Handed Seals: You can perform the Somatic components (hand signs) of a Jutsu with only one free hand. This allows you to cast Jutsu while grappling a creature, holding an object, or wielding a weapon in your other hand. Swift Tactics: You can alter the flow of your chakra to accelerate or delay the speed of your techniques to fit the situation. When you cast a Jutsu that has a casting time of 1 Action, you can change the casting time to 1 Bonus Action for this casting. When you cast a Jutsu that has a casting time of 1 Bonus Action, you can change the casting time to 1 Action for this casting. Cost: To utilize this speed change, you must spend 2 additional Chakra point on top of the Jutsu's standard cost.

Spreading a deck of cards out on a table, a fortune teller smiles at her guest, flipping three of the cards over one by one. With a silky voice and a flourished hand, she speaks of events that have transpired, events that weigh heavy on her guest’s mind, and of events yet to come. Facing down a malevolent spirit, a man in clergical robes watches as it takes control of his companion’s movements. The man thrusts his spirit out towards his ally, wrenching the ghost’s grip away from her mind and allowing her the opportunity to cut the evil being down with a radiant blade. Standing amidst candles and blood, a medium speaks words into the realm beyond life, listening for a response. The soul of an elder, long deceased, pools into existence next to him, giving him advice and information on how to defeat his greatest foe. Regardless of the profession they take up, spiritualists utilize the power of their spirit to influence others, both in this world and the next. Whether they specialize in speaking to those long past, hunting down evil wherever it may rear its head, or taking subtle glances into the future to attempt to shape fate, these masters of souls seek to strengthen their ties to the world, both material and ethereal.

Spiritualists are masters of their own spirits. Similar to monks that seek spiritual peace, spiritualists spend their lives dedicated to cultivating their souls through exercises and manipulation. Unlike monks, who care little for wealth or power, many spiritualists are driven by earthy goals and ambitions. Some spiritualists cultivate their abilities to seek vengeance for being wronged, using their spiritual power to further their own agendas. Some have seen a grim future for themselves, and stop at nothing to prevent seeing that future come to pass. Others still are in the profession for material gain, using the opportunities from reading fortunes and hunting evil to fill their coffers with gold. Adventuring is just another means to an end for many of these individuals, often proving to be a quick (yet perilous) path to power.

Constant training and practice allows a spiritualist to use their souls to manipulate the material plane, offering powerful results. The majority of them draw power from the ethereal plane, manipulating the borders between this world and that to gain strange and unconventional abilities. By linking their souls to entities in the material plane, they can influence such entities in a variety of ways, both beneficially and detrimentally. As they learn to control their spirit more effectively, a spiritualist can exploit and influence the world around them in peculiar ways.

As you make a spiritualist, think of what drives you to cultivate your soul and gain power. Are you trying to get revenge on an evil spirit that hurt your friends or family? Do you want to vanquish anything you percieve as evil on your own terms, without the need to be tied down to oath or order? Do you want to make a fortune as a famed seer, that thousands flock towards to find out what lies ahead for their futures? Your motivations may have a big part in deciding the profession you eventually select for yourself. Besides the things that drive you, it’s also important to decide what extent you’ll go to achieve your ambitions, as well as the methods you might take. Are you willing to make necessary sacrifices to come out ahead? Will you find allies to surround yourself with, and rely on them to assist you with your goals? Maybe you put more of your faith with the dead, and look to them for answers to your problems. Quick Build​ You can make a spiritualist quickly by following these suggestions. First, Wisdom should be your highest ability score, followed by Dexterity or Constitution. Second, choose the Haunted One background.

As a spiritualist, you gain the following class features.
Hit Dice: 1d6 per spiritualist level Hit Points at 1st Level: 6 + your Constitution modifier Hit Points at Higher Levels: 1d6 (or 4) + your Constitution modifier per spiritualist level after 1st

Armor: Light armor Weapons: Daggers, darts, slings, quarterstaffs, light crossbows Tools: none Saving Throws: Wisdom, Charisma Skills: Choose two from Arcana, Deception, Insight, Investigation, Perception, Persuasion, Religion, and Sleight of Hand.

You start with the following equipment, in addition to the equipment granted by your background: (a) a dagger or (b) a quarterstaff (a) a light crossbow and 20 bolts or (b) a sling with 20 bullets (a) a scholar’s pack or (b) an explorer’s pack leather armor and a spiritual focus

At 1st level, you learn to project your own spirit outwards, allowing it to manipulate the material plane. This tether represents your soul’s influence and will be the baseline for your spiritualist abilities. Spiritual Focus​ You employ unorthodox tools through which to channel your spirit. You must have a spiritual focus to use your spirit tether, which can take the form of the following objects: a candle, crystal ball, skull, spirit board, or tarokka deck. Alternatively, you may choose a different object you and your DM agree on. Activating the Spirit Tether​ As a bonus action, you can use your spiritual focus to choose a creature or object other than yourself you can see within 120 feet to latch an invisible spirit rope onto. A creature that can see invisible objects sees a thin, spectral thread directly connecting you to the target. The tether exists in the ethereal plane, and is blocked by any effect that prevents ethereal travel. You must concentrate to maintain the tether as if concentrating on a spell. The spirit rope breaks if you lose concentration, if you are ever more than 120 feet from the target, if it’s blocked in the ethereal plane, if you create another spirit tether, or if you end the connection as a bonus action. When you create your tether or as a bonus action on your turn, you can deal 1d4 force damage to the target. The damage increases when you reach certain levels in this class, increasing to 2d4 at 5th level, 3d4 at 11th level, and 4d4 at 17th level. While you’re tethered to a creature, you can communicate with it telepathically. As long as the creature can understand language, it understands what you communicate even if you don’t share a language and vice versa.

Also at 1st level, you have a heightened sensitivity to spirits and souls in your area. As an action, you can sense the general location of any souls within 30 feet of you, including creatures or objects that contain souls. You learn the direction as well as the quantity of the souls you sense, but cannot determine any other properties. This special vision can see through most barriers, but it is blocked by 1 foot of stone, 1 inch of common metal, a thin sheet of lead, or 3 feet of wood or dirt. This effect lasts for one minute and can only be used again after a short or long rest.

At 2nd level, you can manipulate your spirit tether to accomplish feats unrestrained by your mortal body. The extent to which you can manipulate your spirit without exerting yourself is represented by a number of spirit points. You can spend these spirit points on various spirit arts, which are detailed below. When you spend a spirit point, it is unavailable until you finish a long rest, upon which your spirit is revitalized enough to be utilized further. You can never have more spirit points than shown on the table for your level. Spirit arts can only ever target creatures and objects your spirit tether is connected to. If your spirit tether breaks, the effect of any spirit arts are immediately ended. Some spirit arts require your target to make a saving throw to resist the art’s effects. The saving throw DC is calculated as follows: Art save DC = 8 + your Proficiency Bonus + your Wisdom modifier Corpus Enforcement​ When your tethered target deals damage to you, you can spend 1 spirit point to halve the damage you take. Spirit Jolt​ As an action, you can spend up to 3 spirit points (min. 1) and force the target to make a Charisma saving throw. The target takes 3d6 force damage for each point you spend on a failed save, and half as much on a successful one. Spirit Resonance​ As an action, you can spend 1 spirit point to strengthen the tether between yourself and the tethered target. For one minute, both you and the target can add 1d4 to each saving throw or ability check you make. Corrupt Spirit​ As an action, you can spend 1 spirit point to corrupt the tethered target. It must make a Charisma saving throw. On a failure, the target must roll a d4 and subtract the amount from each ability check, attack roll, or saving throw it makes until the end of your next turn. Spirit Influence​ If the tethered target is a creature, you can use an action to spend 1 spirit point and make the target more malleable to influence. For one minute, your checks made against the target have advantage.

At 2nd level, you can exert your spirit past its normal limits with some effort. When you finish a short rest, you can spend any number of hit dice. Rather than regaining hit points, you regain an amount of spirit points equal to the amount you spent.

At 3rd level, you select a profession to undertake that decides the nature of how you use your spiritual abilities. Your profession grants you features at 3rd level and then again at 6th, 13th, and 18th level. Avenger Exorcist Harbinger Medium Oracle

When you reach 4th level, and again at 8th, 12th, 16th, and 19th level, you can increase one ability score of your choice by 2, or you can increase two ability scores of your choice by 1. As normal, you can’t increase an ability score above 20 using this feature.
At 5th level, if your concentration is broken and you’re not incapacitated, you can spend 1 spirit point to maintain concentration.

At 7th level, when you create a spirit tether, you can target an additional target within range. Whenever you use a spirit art, you can decide if it targets one or both of the targets. If you target multiple creatures or objects with a spirit art, you only have to spend spirit points once. If the tether breaks for a target, only the spirit arts applied to that tether are ended.

At 9th level, you further hone your spirit arts, allowing you to access more refined techniques. You have access to the following spirit arts: Soul Blight​ If your tethered target is a creature, you can use an action and spend 2 spirit points to attempt to taint them. The target must make a constitution saving throw or take 5d6 poison damage at the start of each of their turns. The creature can use an action to purge the blight from their body, ending this spirit art. Tether Swap​ As an action, you can spend 2 spirit points to force the target to make a Charisma save (the target may choose to fail). On a failure, you switch places with the target. If the target is too large to fit in your space or vice versa, the art fails and your spirit points remain unspent. Panic​ As an action, you can spend 2 spirit points to force the target to make a Wisdom saving throw. On a failure, the target is frightened. While frightened, the target must use all of its movement at the start of its turn to move away from you unless there is nowhere else to move. The target can make a Wisdom saving throw at the end of each of its turns, ending this spirit art on a success.
At 10th level, your spirit jolt strengthens in power. Its damage increases to 4d6 force damage for each point you spend.

Once per turn starting at 11th level, when you use a spirit art that takes an action, you can immediately use a different spirit art that also requires an action. You expend spirit points from both arts.

At 14th level, you master control over your spirit, culminating in powerful spirit arts. Spirit Beyond Form​ If the tethered target would reduce you to 0 hit points, you can spend 3 spirit points as a reaction to drop to 1 hit point instead. Soul Surge​ If your tethered target is a creature, you can use your action to spend 3 spirit points and strengthen their soul. During their next turn, they may take an extra action. That action can be used only to take the Attack (one weapon attack only), Dash, Disengage, Hide, or Use an Object action. Oversoul Burst​ If your tethered target is reduced to zero hit points, you can spend 3 spirit points to detonate your soul from its location. Each creature within 10 feet of the target must make a Charisma saving throw. On a failure, the target takes 8d6 force damage, taking half that damage on a success.

At 15th level, your spirit can slip into the ethereal without trouble. You can cast the etherealness spell on yourself without expending a spell slot. Once you do so, you cannot do so again until you finish a long rest or spend 5 spirit points to cast it again.

At 17th level, you can split your soul tether even further. You can now target up to three creatures or objects within range when you use your soul tether. Whenever you use a spirit art, you can choose which targets are affected by it.

At 20th level, you fully master control over your spirit. When you use your soul tether, you can cast your soul out to instantaneously tether to any willing creature on the same plane as yourself. When using your tether in this way, it doesn’t break as a result of being out of range. A creature tethered in this manner can use an action to break the tether at will.

Is that a dragon I see? The Bard Sublime is a master of the cosmic song, a living library of every melody ever hummed and every spell ever woven. At this level of prestige, you are no longer just a performer; you are the conductor of reality itself.
Level 20 Cycle: You must have completed 20 levels of Bard with no multiclassing.

Choose two skills in which you already have Expertise. Your Proficiency Bonus is now tripled for those skills instead of doubled.

These do not count against your spells known. You have mastered the efficiency of the song. You can now grant Bardic Inspiration dice to a number of creatures equal to half your Proficiency Bonus (rounded down) by expending only a single use of your Bardic Inspiration.

You have mastered two more of the Words of Creation: the words of pain and rest. You always have the power word pain and power word stun spells prepared, and they do not count against the number of spells you can have prepared. When you cast either of these spells, you can target a second creature with it, provided that the second creature is within 10 feet of the first target. Additionally, your inspiration carries a lingering, harmonic echo. Whenever an ally successfully uses one of your Bardic Inspiration dice, you can choose another ally within 30 feet of the first. That chosen ally gains a Bardic Inspiration die of the same size, which expires at the end of their next turn.

Cheaters go by many names; swindlers, con-artists, charlatans. Whatever they may call you, whoever you might be perceived as, you’ll always be the first to let the world know that the cards in your hand are there entirely legitimately— you couldn’t have stacked the deck, the dealer shuffled beforehand! You weren’t responsible for the incomprehensibly lucky die rolls, either— you were borrowing the dealer’s dice, after all. Oh, and the drinking game you outlasted the dwarf barbarian in? You couldn’t have watered your drink down, the dealer poured it out for you! …What? You’re being accused of paying off the dealer? Poppycock. Features: 3rd Level - Swindler’s Luck 9th Level - Loaded Dice 13th Level - Sure Shot 17th Level - Don of Con

At 3rd level, luck seems to appear whenever it benefits you, almost as if you’re cheating. Whenever you make a roll with advantage, you may meddle with the roll, forgoing that advantage, and roll normally. The next time you roll without advantage, you roll with advantage.

At 9th level, you cheat act with more finesse, giving you more control over your actions. Whenever you make a roll with advantage, you may forgo that advantage to create a loaded die. You may store a number of loaded dice equal to half your proficiency bonus, rounded down. These loaded dice disappear on a short or long rest. Whenever you roll an attack roll, ability check, or saving throw, you may spend one of your loaded dice to give yourself advantage on that roll. You may only spend one loaded die per turn.

By 13th level, your “luck” is far too consistent to be inconspicuous. When you roll with advantage, you may forgo that advantage to add +3 to the roll’s total. If the roll succeeds, you gain one loaded die.

At 17th level, it’s quite clear you’ve been cheating all this time, some way, somehow. On the bright side, you don’t have to hide it anymore— whenever you miss with an attack roll, you can spend 3 loaded dice to turn that miss into a hit. When you fail a saving throw, you can spend 2 loaded dice to succeed automatically. When you fail an ability check, you can spend 1 loaded die to make the result 20.

A master of powder, precision, and pressure. Gunslingers are elite martial combatants who specialize in firearms. Whether a patient sharpshooter, a lightning-fast revolver duelist, or a battlefield suppressor, the Gunslinger dominates ranged combat through discipline, tactical positioning, and superior weapon mastery.

The effects of these shots are until the end of the targets turn if they hit. The DC for your Called Shots is equal to 8 + proficiency bonus + Dexterity modifier: Suppressing Shot: Target’s speed reduced by 10 ft. Disarming Shot: Target drops one held object (Str save).

Level 1 Choose 2 weapons you have proficiency with to have complete Mastery over and be able to use their Mastery property. During a long rest you may practice with a different weapon and swap 1 weapon mastery out with a weapon you are proficient with.

Level 2 As a bonus action, enter one stance. You may switch stances as a bonus action. The duration is for 1 minute. If knocked unconscious or incapacitated your stance breaks. Spend 1 Grit to enter or change stances. 1 Stance can be active at a time. Deadeye Stance​ If you do not move this turn, your first hit with a Sights weapon deals +1d6 damage. Skirmisher Stance​ After making an attack, you may move up to 10 feet without provoking opportunity attacks once per turn. Brace Stance​ If you did not move on your turn, gain +2 AC until the start of your next turn. You may make opportunity attacks with firearms at targets about to leave your weapons normal range.

Level 5 You can attack twice when you take the attack action on your turn. At level 14, you can attack three times.

An Undead Sovereign commands death beyond the boundaries of ordinary necromancy. Beasts, giants, dragons, and extraplanar creatures become vessels for their power. Their servants sustain them, their command strengthens the dead, and their own body grows increasingly resistant to death.

You must complete a pure first cycle—20 levels in a single class—with one of the following subclasses: Wizard: School of Necromancy. Druid: Circle of Spores. Cleric: Death Domain. Paladin: Oathbreaker. Warlock: The Undead, The Undying, or The Hexblade. Other subclasses require staff approval to qualify.

Hit Dice: 1d8 per Undead Sovereign level. Hit Points: 1d8 (or 5) + your Constitution modifier per Undead Sovereign level. Additional Proficiencies: Two skills of your choice from Arcana, History, Insight, Medicine, and Religion. Choose Intelligence, Wisdom, or Charisma as your Sovereign ability when you enter this class. It is used by your Undead Sovereign spells and features. Sovereign save DC = 8 + your proficiency bonus + your Sovereign ability modifier. Spell attack modifier = your proficiency bonus + your Sovereign ability modifier.

When you enter Undead Sovereign, you may choose an additional subclass from the class in which you completed your first cycle. You retain your existing subclass. You gain the additional subclass’s features when your Undead Sovereign class level reaches the level at which the parent class normally grants them. For example, an additional wizard subclass grants its features at Undead Sovereign class levels 2, 6, 10, and 14—progression levels 22, 26, 30, and 34. When an additional subclass feature refers to your level in its parent class, use your Undead Sovereign class level. Your original subclass continues to use your actual levels in its parent class. This progression grants only the additional subclass’s features. It does not grant other parent-class features, spell slots, or increases to parent-class resources unless the additional subclass feature explicitly grants them.

Your progression level equals 20 + your Undead Sovereign class levels. All feature levels below refer to progression level. Your additional subclass follows the Subclass Selection and Progression rules above. Each spell must be of a level no higher than the slot level shown in the table. Casting a spell does not remove it from your prepared spells.

Your Sovereign ability is your spellcasting ability for these spells. They use your Sovereign save DC and spell attack modifier. You can use an arcane focus or holy symbol as a spellcasting focus for your Undead Sovereign spells.

You can use these slots to cast your prepared Undead Sovereign spells or spells you know or have prepared through another class, following that spell’s normal casting rules. You can also expend these slots for Undead Sovereign features, including Draconic Breath recovery and additional uses of Grave Renewal. Slots from your other classes can also pay these costs.

You perform a 10-minute ritual over eligible corpses within 30 feet of you. Each rises as an undead under your control, using its original stat block with the changes below. A corpse must retain enough of its body to support its attacks and movement. Creatures with class levels and remains produced by temporary summoning effects are ineligible. The ritual does not create equipment.

New creature types are added to those already unlocked. Reanimation Improvements increase your limits as shown below. Progression Level New Creature Types Maximum CR per Creature Total CR Budget 21 Humanoids, Beasts 2 4 25 Monstrosities 4 8 29 Giants 6 12 33 Dragons 14 16 37 Fiends, Celestials 18 20 You can control up to twice your proficiency bonus in undead through Greater Reanimation. Each must meet your maximum CR per creature, and their combined CR cannot exceed your total CR budget. Use each creature’s original CR before reanimation, counting CR below 1 as CR 1. The total CR of creatures you animate between long rests also cannot exceed your budget. Destroying or releasing undead does not refund this allowance. Renewing control does not spend it. These limits apply only to Greater Reanimation.

Use the creature’s original stat block with these changes: Its creature type becomes Undead. Its hit-point maximum becomes half its original average hit points, rounded down (minimum 1). Apply bonuses afterward. It rises with this many hit points. Its Intelligence becomes 6 if it was higher. It understands your languages and can speak any languages it could speak in life. It gains immunity to poison damage and the poisoned condition. It requires no air, food, drink, or sleep. It retains its size, Armor Class, movement, senses, other ability scores, saving throw and skill bonuses, damage resistances, damage immunities, damage vulnerabilities, and condition immunities. It retains weapon attacks and Multiattack. Retained attacks keep their damage, reach, range, and any effects that grapple, restrain through a grapple, knock prone, or swallow. They lose all other additional effects. Multiattack allows only retained weapon attacks. It loses all original traits and all other original actions, bonus actions, and reactions, including spellcasting, Legendary Resistance, legendary actions, mythic actions, and lair actions. If it is proficient with a weapon it gains the ability to use that weapons mastery. It can take ordinary actions such as Dash, Disengage, and Dodge, make opportunity attacks, and use abilities granted by Undead Sovereign. Prepare its modified stat block when you animate it and reuse that stat block during play.
Undead created through Greater Reanimation take their turns immediately after yours. You choose their order each round. Each has its own movement, action, bonus action, and reaction.

Your control lasts for 24 hours. Another 10-minute ritual renews control over any number of these undead within 30 feet for a further 24 hours. You can release an undead at any time without an action. If released or your control expires, it becomes an inanimate corpse. This feature cannot take control of another creature’s undead.

As a bonus action, mentally issue orders to any or all undead under your control within 60 feet. They follow those orders on their turns until completed or replaced. Without orders, undead created through Greater Reanimation defend themselves. Orders can direct any action available to the undead, including Draconic Breath. The undead must expend any required use. This replaces their usual command range and action requirement. It does not extend their existence or your control. At progression level 27, the range increases to 120 feet. When you use this bonus action, you can also choose one commanded undead. It can immediately use its reaction to move up to half its speed without provoking opportunity attacks. This movement still requires your bonus action when you gain Deathless Command.

When you or an undead under your control reduces a creature within 60 feet of you to 0 hit points, you can regain hit points equal to your Sovereign ability modifier plus twice your proficiency bonus. Once you use this feature, you cannot use it again until the start of your next turn. Constructs, Undead, and creatures you summoned or control do not trigger this healing. You cannot benefit from both this feature and Grim Harvest on the same turn. At progression level 35, the healing increases to your Sovereign ability modifier plus three times your proficiency bonus. Any healing beyond your hit-point maximum becomes temporary hit points, which last for 1 minute.

You gain resistance to necrotic and poison damage, and advantage on saving throws to avoid or end the poisoned condition. At progression level 31, you become immune to poison damage and the poisoned condition.

At progression levels 24, 28, 32, 36, and 39, increase one ability score by 2, or two ability scores by 1 each. You cannot increase a score above 20 using this feature. Any option to choose a feat instead follows TWR’s rules.

Weapon attacks made by undead under your control count as magical for overcoming resistance and immunity to nonmagical attacks and damage. When one of these undead hits with a weapon attack, you can replace all of that attack’s damage types with necrotic damage. Choose before rolling damage; the amount is unchanged.

During a 10-minute ritual, designate up to your proficiency bonus in undead you created and currently control as your Eternal Legion. Your control over them no longer expires with time. This does not extend a temporary summon’s duration or prevent another effect from ending your control. Undead created through Greater Reanimation still count toward its limits. You can replace members during another 10-minute ritual. Removing a member ends this indefinite control; any unexpired control from its original spell or feature remains. You cannot have more members of your Eternal Legion than your proficiency bonus.

When you or an undead under your control deals necrotic damage to a creature, you can prevent that creature from regaining hit points until the start of your next turn. Once you use this effect, you cannot use it again until the start of your next turn. You can also cast animate dead at 3rd level and create undead at 6th level once each without expending a spell slot or preparing the spell. You regain both castings when you finish a long rest. Their normal components, casting times, and restrictions apply. These castings use your Sovereign ability. This feature does not add create undead to your prepared spells or grant a 6th-level spell slot. Undead created by these spells follow their normal rules, except where another Undead Sovereign feature explicitly changes them.

You become immune to necrotic damage. Your hit-point maximum cannot be reduced, and you cannot be aged magically. When you would drop to 0 hit points without being killed outright, you can destroy an undead under your control within 120 feet that has at least 1 hit point. You drop to 1 hit point instead. This requires no action. Once you preserve yourself this way, you cannot do so again until you finish a long rest.

Undead created through Greater Reanimation gain a bonus to their hit-point maximum equal to twice your Undead Sovereign class level. Apply this bonus after halving their original hit points. The bonus updates as you gain levels in this class.

When you animate a dragon through Greater Reanimation, choose one damaging breath weapon it possessed in life that used a cone or line. If it had an eligible breath weapon, it gains the following action: Draconic Breath. As an action, the dragon exhales in a 30-foot cone or a 60-foot-long, 5-foot-wide line, matching the chosen breath’s shape. Each creature in the area must make a saving throw against your Sovereign save DC, using the original breath’s saving throw ability. A creature takes 8d8 damage on a failed save, or half as much on a success. The breath retains its original damage type, but loses its additional effects and recharge. Shared Breath Uses​ You have three uses of Draconic Breath shared among all dragons under your control that possess this action. Each activation expends one use. You regain all expended uses when you finish a long rest. As a bonus action, you can expend a spell slot of 3rd level or higher to restore one expended use, up to a maximum of three available uses. Creating, replacing, or reanimating undead does not restore uses.

Starting at 34th level, you can use magic to bring undead under your control, even those created by other necromancers. As an action, you can choose two undead that you can see within 60 feet of you. That creature must make a Charisma saving throw against your undead sovereign spell save DC. If it succeeds, you can't use this feature on it again. If it fails, it becomes friendly to you and obeys your commands until you use this feature again. Intelligent undead are harder to control in this way. If the target has an Intelligence of 8 or higher, it has advantage on the saving throw. If it fails the saving throw and has an Intelligence of 12 or higher, it can repeat the saving throw at the end of every hour until it succeeds and breaks free.

When you use Greater Grim Harvest, you can give its healing to one undead under your control within 60 feet instead of yourself. Any healing beyond that undead’s hit-point maximum becomes temporary hit points, which last for 1 minute. You can do so even if you are at your hit-point maximum. Additionally, as an action, choose a number of undead under your control within 60 feet up to your Sovereign ability modifier (minimum of one). Each regains hit points equal to twice your Undead Sovereign class level. You can use this action once without expending a spell slot, regaining that use when you finish a long rest. Additional uses each require a spell slot of 5th level or higher, expended as part of the action. Neither benefit restores a destroyed undead.

You can issue orders through Grave Command anywhere on the same plane of existence without using an action or bonus action. The reaction movement granted by Grave Command at progression level 27 gains this range but still requires your bonus action and the undead’s reaction. Sovereign Command also gains this range but still requires your action action.This feature does not extend an undead’s existence or the duration of your control.
Your Sovereign ability score and Constitution score each increase by 4, to a maximum of 30.

A Complete Class for Fifth Edition An elf recites the motions for the simplest spell she knows, repeating them until she knows they are perfect. With a single precise stroke she unleashes a wave of arcane energy, focused into a searing blue beam. A tiefling waves her hands to conjure floating greatswords of humming blue energy that dance about in mesmerizing and deadly arcs. One blade takes on an aspect of fire, the other lightning, as she begins to cleave through the goblinoid horde. Waving a black-and-red checkered banner, a dragonborn king charges into the fore. At his sides are warmages of all houses, a chessboard of elite arcanists poised to turn the tide of battle. Cantrip Masters​ While other spellcasters aspire to grander and more complex spells, warmages refine and master the most fundamental magic: cantrips. A warmage wields magic the way a warrior uses a sword, a bow or an axe — as a weapon to be perfected, not as an unknowable force to be feared. In contrast to sorcerers and wizards, their magic is a trainable skill, one that can be mastered by almost anyone with discipline and aptitude. Warmages therefore stand among the most fearsome of spellcasters while commanding only the most rudimentary of spells. A warmage does not out-damage a wizard. She out-manoeuvres one. The same fire bolt that a first-year apprentice throws becomes, in a warmage’s hands, a cone of flame, a spray of embers that catches three goblins at once, a shot that punches through a stone pillar, or a blast that knocks a troll flat on its back — because she has spent years learning what the spell can be made to do rather than searching for a bigger one. Strategic Geniuses​ Warmages have a long and storied history as masterful strategists and tacticians, both in grand battles and in personal skirmishes. If a warmage is outgunned or outnumbered, they will try to outthink their foes, which works more often than not. Warmages demonstrate an efficient kind of pragmatism, owing perhaps to their ability to solve many problems with just a few magical tools. Aligned Free Agents​ While some warmages are fully self-taught, the majority join a house: a loose confederation of warmages who practise together and share secrets of the trade. Houses teach invaluable battlefield strategy, but each house also touts its own brands of tactics and styles of magical trickery. The House of Knights emphasises armour and martial prowess; the House of Kings emphasises battlefield command. By way of metaphor, houses that value honour and teamwork above all else brand themselves after games of strategy — the Bishops, Kings, Knights, Pawns and Rooks — whereas those who epitomise self-reliance name themselves for games of chance. This division dates back to the earliest warmage masters. Legend has it that the first two masters separated when one decided to found a college; the other, out of spite, built a casino outside its grounds. The gamblers of that casino are the House of Fortune, and they have never once apologised. Creating a Warmage​ Warmages come from all walks of life, so as you build yours, consider where you first learned the fundamentals of magic. You might have picked up cantrips from a fellow adventurer or in the early stages of wizarding training. You could be entirely self-taught. Choose an Arcane Initiation that best fits your character’s history with magic. Consider also how you feel about magic as a whole. Are you envious of other spellcasters, or confident you could best them regardless? Did you once pine to be a wizard, but find you could never muster enough true magic to form a spell slot? Did you choose warmagistry to hone your talents to their absolute peak, or to wield power no warrior can equal? Lastly, consider your prospective House. Though you do not choose one until 3rd level, your aspirations might shape which you favour. If you would like to dabble in greater arcane magic, the House of Bishops is the best fit. If the clashing of swords at the frontline piques your interest, consider the House of Knights. If you would rather not be told which of the two you are, the House of Pawns will have you. Quick Build​ Make Intelligence your highest ability score, followed by Constitution. Make Strength your third highest if you plan to take the House of Knights, or Dexterity otherwise. Choose the chill touch, force dart, force weapon and phantom grapnel cantrips, and the Adventurer Arcane Initiation. Take the Blaster or Resistive fighting style, and pick any background that emphasises magical discipline. At 2nd level, take the Blasting Flourish and Mystical Armor.

As a warmage, you gain the following class features. The Warmage table​ Level Prof. Features Cantrips Known Overcharge Uses Tricks Known 1st +2 Spellcasting, Arcane Initiation, Arcane Fighting Style 4 — — 2nd +2 Warmage Edge, Warmage Tricks, Cantrip Flourishes 4 — 2 3rd +2 Warmage House 5 — 3 4th +2 Ability Score Improvement 5 — 3 5th +3 Overcharge 6 2 4 6th +3 Deflective Instinct 6 2 4 7th +3 Warmage House feature 6 2 5 8th +3 Ability Score Improvement 6 2 5 9th +4 Overcharge (3 uses) 7 3 6 10th +4 Warmage House feature 7 3 6 11th +4 Greater Overcharges, Edge Improvement 7 3 7 12th +4 Ability Score Improvement 7 3 7 13th +5 Overcharge (4 uses) 8 4 8 14th +5 Strategic Deflection 8 4 8 15th +5 Warmage House feature 8 4 9 16th +5 Ability Score Improvement 8 4 9 17th +6 Master Overcharges, Edge Improvement 9 5 10 18th +6 Warmage House feature 9 5 10 19th +6 Ability Score Improvement 9 5 10 20th +6 Master Warmage 10 5 10
Hit Dice: 1d8 per warmage level. Hit Points at 1st Level: 8 + your Constitution modifier. Hit Points at Higher Levels: 1d8 (or 5) + your Constitution modifier per warmage level after 1st.

Armor: Light armor Weapons: Simple weapons Tools: One artisan’s kit of your choice, one gaming set of your choice Saving Throws: Constitution, Intelligence Skills: Choose two from Acrobatics, Animal Handling, Arcana, Athletics, History, Investigation, Medicine, Perception and Survival

You start with the following equipment, in addition to the equipment granted by your background: Leather armor, a dagger, and any simple weapon (a) a component pouch or (b) an arcane focus (a) an explorer’s pack or (b) a scholar’s pack A gaming set
At 1st level you begin to learn the simple yet potent brand of spellcasting for which warmages are known.

You know four cantrips of your choice from the warmage spell list. You learn additional warmage cantrips of your choice at higher levels, as shown in the Cantrips Known column of the Warmage table. Additionally, when you gain a level in this class you can replace one warmage cantrip you know with another from the warmage spell list.

Intelligence is your spellcasting ability for your warmage spells, since you learn your spells through practice and mental discipline. You use your Intelligence whenever a spell refers to your spellcasting ability, and you use your Intelligence modifier when setting the saving throw DC for a warmage spell and when making an attack roll with one. Spell save DC = 8 + your proficiency bonus + your Intelligence modifier Spell attack modifier = your proficiency bonus + your Intelligence modifier
You can use an arcane focus as a spellcasting focus for your warmage spells.

Warmages come from all backgrounds and walks of life. At 1st level, choose where you first learned the basics of magic. The two cantrips your initiation grants do not count against your number of cantrips known. Adventurer. You picked up your magic informally by travelling with a dozen different mages over the years. You learn mage hand and ray of frost. Circus Performer. You learned a few simple tricks to participate in a sideshow act. You learn dancing lights and minor illusion. Eldritch Event. An influx of insidious magic left an imprint on you. You learn chill touch and message. Mercenary. You mastered the fundamentals of war magic to engage in battle with similarly armed arcanists. You learn arc blade and true strike. Self-Taught. You taught yourself the fundamentals from a dusty tome or an abandoned scroll. You learn fire bolt and light. Survival. To stay alive in the wilderness, you taught yourself to cast simple spells. You learn druidcraft and shillelagh. Temple. A monastery or temple educated you in the ways of gentle healing magic. You learn sacred flame and spare the dying. Tower Apprentice. You apprenticed under a spellcaster who taught you the fundamentals of arcana. You learn prestidigitation and shocking grasp.

Warmages learn that magic is the purest of weapons and can be wielded as easily as any other. At 1st level, choose one of the following fighting styles. Blaster. You gain a +1 bonus to the saving throw DCs of your warmage spells. Deflector. When you have at least one hand free and a creature hits you with a spell attack or a ranged weapon attack, you can use your reaction to add 3 to your Armor Class against that attack, potentially causing it to miss. Resistive. While you are wearing light armor or are under the effects of the mage armor spell, you gain a +1 bonus to your Armor Class. Sniper. You gain a +1 bonus to ranged spell attack rolls, and your warmage cantrips ignore half cover. Striker. When you hit a creature with a cantrip that requires a melee attack and you exceed the target’s Armor Class by 5 or more, or you score a critical hit, you can add your proficiency bonus to the damage roll.

Starting at 2nd level, you can channel raw arcane pressure into the cantrips you have perfected. Once on each of your turns when you deal damage with a warmage cantrip, choose one of that cantrip’s damage rolls and add your Intelligence modifier to it. At 11th level, you can add your Intelligence modifier to two of that cantrip’s damage rolls, and at 17th level, three. If the cantrip has fewer damage rolls than that, add your Intelligence modifier to the same roll for each remaining application. For example, a 17th-level warmage casting fire bolt makes one damage roll and so deals 4d10 + three times her Intelligence modifier. The same warmage casting magic daggers makes four separate damage rolls, and adds her Intelligence modifier to three of them.

Also at 2nd level, you learn to hang a small piece of battlefield craft off the end of a cantrip. Certain warmage tricks are Flourishes, identified as such in their descriptions. Once on each of your turns, when you deal damage to a creature with a warmage cantrip, you can apply one Flourish you know to that creature. You can apply only one Flourish on each of your turns, no matter how many you know. A Flourish requires no action and can be applied in the same turn you use Warmage Edge or an Overcharge.

Beginning at 2nd level, you learn to use warmage tricks: special techniques that alter the way you fight, move and cast your spells. You learn two tricks of your choice for which you meet the prerequisites, and you learn additional tricks as shown in the Tricks Known column of the Warmage table. Flourishes are tricks and count against this number. When you gain a level in this class, you can choose one of the tricks you know and replace it with another trick for which you meet the prerequisites. A level prerequisite refers to your level in this class.

Upon reaching 3rd level, you choose a Warmage House that teaches you a suite of magical strategies: the House of Bishops, Fortune, Kings, Knights, Pawns or Rooks. Your choice grants you features at 3rd level and again at 7th, 10th, 15th and 18th level.

When you reach 4th level, and again at 8th, 12th, 16th and 19th level, you can increase one ability score of your choice by 2, or you can increase two ability scores of your choice by 1. As normal, you can’t increase an ability score above 20 using this feature.

Starting at 5th level, you can force more out of a cantrip than it was ever built to carry — not more power, but a different shape entirely. You have a number of Overcharge uses shown in the Overcharge Uses column of the Warmage table. You regain all expended uses when you finish a short or long rest. When you cast a warmage cantrip, you can expend one use of Overcharge to apply one Overcharge option you know to that casting. You know all of the Lesser Overcharges from 5th level, you learn the Greater Overcharges at 11th level, and you learn the Master Overcharges at 17th level. Where an Overcharge calls for a saving throw, the DC equals your spell save DC. You can apply only one Overcharge to a single casting of a cantrip until 20th level, and applying an Overcharge does not change the cantrip’s casting time unless the Overcharge says so. The Overcharge options are described in their own section, following the Flourishes.

At 6th level, you learn to shed hostile magic rather than merely endure it. When you succeed on a saving throw against a spell or other magical effect that would still deal half damage to you on a successful save, you take no damage from it instead.

Starting at 14th level, when a creature casts a spell that forces you to make a saving throw to avoid damage, you can use your reaction to attempt to redirect some of the spell’s energy to a new target. If you succeed on your saving throw against the spell, choose another creature you can see within the spell’s range or up to 30 feet away from you, whichever is closer, to make a saving throw against your spell save DC. The chosen creature can be the original spellcaster. On a failed save, the creature suffers the effects of the spell as if you had cast it and it had been the original target or been within the area of the spell. Once you use this feature, you can’t use it again until you finish a short or long rest.

At 20th level, you reach the pinnacle of your warmage prowess. You can apply two different Overcharges to the same casting of a cantrip, expending one use of Overcharge for each. In addition, when you roll initiative and have no uses of Overcharge remaining, you regain two uses.

To take a level in this class as a multiclass character, you must have an Intelligence score of 13 or higher. You gain proficiency with light armor, simple weapons and one gaming set of your choice. Your warmage cantrips do not count against the number of cantrips you know from other classes, and levels in this class do not contribute to your spellcaster level for the purposes of the Multiclass Spellcaster table — except for levels in the House of Bishops, which count as one third of a level, rounded down, in the same manner as an Eldritch Knight.

Each Flourish below is a warmage trick. You apply one Flourish on each of your turns, when a warmage cantrip you cast deals damage to a creature. Each Flourish requires the cantrip to have dealt damage of the listed type to that creature. Where a Flourish calls for a saving throw, the DC equals your spell save DC. Blasting Flourish​ Prerequisite: force damage. You push the creature up to 10 feet away from you in a straight line. Concussive Flourish​ Prerequisite: thunder damage. A 15-foot-diameter sphere of magical silence, as per the silence spell, is centred on the creature or on yourself (your choice) and lasts until the start of your next turn. Corrosive Flourish​ Prerequisite: acid damage. The acid eats into the creature’s defences. The next attack roll made against it before the start of your next turn treats its Armor Class as 2 lower. Draining Flourish​ Prerequisite: necrotic or poison damage. You siphon some of the creature’s life force and gain temporary hit points equal to your Intelligence modifier, which last for 1 minute. Temporary hit points from this Flourish don’t stack with themselves. Explosive Flourish​ Prerequisite: fire damage. The fire detonates. Each creature within 5 feet of the target other than you and the target must succeed on a Dexterity saving throw or take half the fire damage dealt to the target. Icy Flourish​ Prerequisite: cold damage. Until the start of your next turn, the creature’s speed is reduced by 10 feet and it takes a −2 penalty to the next attack roll it makes. Radiant Flourish​ Prerequisite: radiant damage. Until the start of your next turn, the creature sheds dim light in a 10-foot radius and can’t benefit from being invisible or from being hidden. Rending Flourish​ Prerequisite: bludgeoning, piercing or slashing damage. The creature can’t take reactions until the start of your next turn. Static Flourish​ Prerequisite: lightning damage. You sap part of the energy into a charge that clings to your body until the start of your next turn. While charged, you can use your reaction when you take damage from a creature you can see within 5 feet of you to deal lightning damage equal to your Intelligence modifier to that creature. Suppressing Flourish​ Prerequisite: 5th level, any damage type. The creature has disadvantage on the next attack roll it makes against a target other than you before the start of your next turn.

You expend one use of Overcharge to apply one of these options to a warmage cantrip as you cast it. Where an Overcharge calls for a saving throw, the DC equals your spell save DC. Lesser Overcharges​ You know all of these from 5th level. Barrage​ If the cantrip requires a single attack roll, make one additional attack roll against a different creature within 15 feet of the original target. On a hit, that creature takes the cantrip’s damage. Warmage Edge can enhance the damage of only one of the two attacks. Breach​ The cantrip ignores cover, and the target’s resistance to the cantrip’s damage type has no effect against it. If the cantrip damages an object, it deals double damage to it. Concussion​ The target must succeed on a Strength saving throw or be pushed 10 feet away from you and knocked prone. Quicken​ You cast the cantrip as a bonus action instead of an action. You can use this Overcharge only once on each of your turns. Refract​ A cantrip that targets a single creature instead fills a 15-foot cone originating from you. Each creature in the cone must make a Dexterity saving throw, taking the cantrip’s damage on a failed save and half as much damage on a successful one. Warmage Edge can enhance the damage against only one creature. If the cantrip normally requires an attack roll, you make no attack roll when you use this Overcharge. Snare​ The target must make a Strength or Dexterity saving throw (its choice). On a failed save, its speed becomes 0 until the start of your next turn. Greater Overcharges​ You learn these at 11th level, in addition to the Lesser Overcharges. Displace​ After the cantrip resolves, either you or the target teleports up to 30 feet to an unoccupied space that you can see. An unwilling target can resist with a Charisma saving throw. Overload​ Treat each of the cantrip’s damage dice against one target of your choice as having rolled the highest number possible. You can’t apply this Overcharge to a cantrip that has scored a critical hit. Rupture​ Until the start of your next turn, the target has disadvantage on the next saving throw it makes and it can’t regain hit points. Master Overcharges​ You learn these at 17th level, in addition to the Lesser and Greater Overcharges. Cataclysm​ A cantrip that targets a single creature instead fills a 20-foot-radius sphere centred on a point you can see within the cantrip’s range. Each creature in the area must make a Dexterity saving throw, taking the cantrip’s damage on a failed save and half as much damage on a successful one. Warmage Edge can enhance the damage against only one creature. If the cantrip normally requires an attack roll, you make no attack roll when you use this Overcharge. Unmake​ Until the end of your next turn, the target’s Armor Class is reduced by 2 and it has disadvantage on attack rolls.

The tricks below are presented in alphabetical order. The ten Flourishes described earlier are also warmage tricks. If a trick has prerequisites, you must meet them to choose it; you can choose the trick at the same time you meet its prerequisites. Bishop’s Maneuver​ Prerequisites: 10th level, House of Bishops You can take the Disengage action as a bonus action. When you do so, your walking speed increases by 10 feet until the end of your turn. Blinding Light​ Prerequisite: light cantrip When you use the light cantrip to target an object you are holding, you can direct a flare at a creature you can see within 10 feet of you. That creature must make a Constitution saving throw against your spell save DC, and on a failed save it is blinded until the start of your next turn. After a creature has failed a saving throw against this trick, it has advantage on all saving throws against it for the next 24 hours. Castle​ Prerequisites: 10th level, House of Rooks As an action, you can choose a willing Small or Medium creature you can see within 120 feet of you. You both teleport, swapping places. Once you use this trick, you can’t use it again until you finish a short or long rest. Chivalrous Presence​ Prerequisite: House of Knights You gain proficiency in the Insight and Persuasion skills, and you have advantage on ability checks you make to interact with nobility. Commander’s Steed​ Prerequisite: House of Kings You learn the find steed spell. You can cast it once without expending a spell slot, and you regain the ability to do so when you finish a long rest. Your steed is more resilient than most: its hit point maximum increases by an amount equal to your warmage level. Encryptogram​ Prerequisite: cryptogram cantrip Your knowledge of ciphers has improved your magically clandestine communications. When you cast cryptogram, its limit is 20 characters instead of 8, and only the specified recipient can read the message. Extended Range​ Whenever you cast a warmage cantrip that has a range of 5 feet or greater, its range is doubled. Field Medic​ Prerequisite: House of Bishops You learn the spare the dying cantrip, which doesn’t count against your number of cantrips known. Additionally, when you cast spare the dying on a creature that has 0 hit points, the target regains 1 hit point and gains temporary hit points equal to your warmage level, which last for 1 minute. Once a creature regains hit points from this trick, it can’t do so again until it finishes a long rest. Flexible Range​ Being within 5 feet of a hostile creature doesn’t impose disadvantage on your ranged spell attack rolls. Additionally, when you cast a warmage cantrip that requires a melee spell attack, its range increases to 10 feet. Fold​ Prerequisites: 10th level, House of Fortune You have learned to accept defeat graciously. As a reaction when you are hit by an attack, you can expend three Fate Dice to cast the shield spell without expending a spell slot. Once you use this trick, you can’t use it again until you finish a short or long rest. Gamble​ Prerequisites: House of Fortune, cheat cantrip You are always under the effects of the cheat cantrip. Additionally, when you miss with an attack roll or you fail an ability check or saving throw, you can reroll the d20 and must use the new roll. Once you use this ability, you can’t use it again until you finish a short or long rest. Infinite Variation​ Prerequisite: prestidigitation cantrip You have become exceptionally skilled at using prestidigitation to mimic other spells. When you cast prestidigitation, you can use it to emulate the effects of any cantrip that doesn’t deal damage from the bard, sorcerer, warlock or wizard spell list, even one you don’t know. To do so, you must succeed on a DC 15 Intelligence (Arcana) check, otherwise the spell fails. Intelligence is your spellcasting ability for a cantrip cast using this trick, and it counts as a warmage cantrip for you. Knight’s Aegis​ Prerequisites: 10th level, House of Knights, force buckler cantrip When you cast the force buckler cantrip, it lasts until the end of your next turn and it doesn’t end early if you are hit by an attack. Leading Edge Tactics​ Prerequisite: House of Kings You always have a plan when engaging the enemy. Attacks against you have disadvantage during the first round of combat. You can’t use this feature when you are surprised. Lieutenant’s Demand​ Prerequisites: 10th level, House of Kings You can cast the command spell without expending a spell slot, using your Intelligence as your spellcasting ability for it. Once you use this trick, you can’t use it again until you finish a short or long rest. Mage Hand Knack​ Prerequisite: mage hand cantrip Your skill with mage hand allows you to use it as an extension of yourself. When you cast the spell, and as a bonus action on your subsequent turns, you can use one of the following effects with the hand. Press. The hand pushes against a Large or smaller creature within 5 feet of it. Choose a direction away from that creature. Every foot of movement in that direction while the hand is pressing against it costs the creature 1 extra foot of movement. The hand continues to press until the spell ends or you use your bonus action to use a different effect. Punch. The hand strikes one creature or object within 5 feet of it. Make a melee spell attack for the hand. On a hit, the target takes 1d6 force damage. Seize. The hand grabs a Small or smaller creature and attempts to grapple it. The creature must succeed on a Strength (Athletics) or Dexterity (Acrobatics) check of its choice against your spell save DC or be grappled by the hand. The hand continues to grapple until the target uses an action to break the grapple on its turn, the spell ends, or you use your bonus action to use a different effect. Minor Shadow Illusion​ Prerequisite: minor illusion cantrip When you create the image of an object in an unoccupied space using minor illusion, you can fill it with fibres of shadowstuff, causing it to become partially real. No matter what form the semi-real object takes, it must be no larger than a 5-foot cube. It has AC 10 and 5 hit points and it weighs 5 pounds. You can have only one semi-real illusion at a time, and while it exists the cantrip requires your concentration. The illusion can’t replicate a creature, but it can deal damage to a creature within its 5-foot cube. If the illusion is of an object that could deal damage, a creature that enters the object’s cube for the first time on a turn or begins its turn there must make an Intelligence saving throw against your spell save DC, taking 1d6 damage of a type appropriate to the illusion on a failed save. This damage increases to 2d6 at 5th level, 3d6 at 11th level and 4d6 at 17th level. This damage can’t trigger Warmage Edge, a Flourish or an Overcharge. Mystical Armor​ You can cast the mage armor spell on yourself at will, without expending a spell slot and without spell components. Mystical Athlete​ Prerequisite: quickstep or springheel cantrip When you cast quickstep, your speed increases by 20 feet instead of 10 feet. When you cast springheel, your jumping distance increases by 20 feet instead of 10 feet. If you know both of these cantrips, you can cast both of them as part of the same bonus action. Mystical Vision​ You can cast the detect magic spell at will, without expending a spell slot. Mystical Weaponmaster​ Prerequisite: force weapon or magic daggers cantrip When you roll a 1 on the d20 for an attack roll with force weapon or magic daggers, you can reroll the die and must use the new roll. Phantom Hookshot​ Prerequisite: phantom grapnel cantrip You can cast the phantom grapnel cantrip as a bonus action. If you do so, its range is reduced to 15 feet. When you cast the spell as an action, creatures are pulled an extra 10 feet toward you by the spell. Rapid Fortification​ Prerequisite: mending cantrip You can cast the mending cantrip as an action or a bonus action. If you cast it as an action, you can use one of the following effects. You restore a single nonmagical object, such as a door, cart or window, to pristine condition if at least half of its parts are present. The object can be no larger than 10 cubic feet, or 1 cubic foot if it is exceptionally complex, such as a clock. You create simple fortifications, such as sealing a door shut, adding wooden planks to a window, or building a short stone wall no larger than 10 cubic feet. You must have the materials present to use this ability. Severe Cantrip​ When a creature rolls a 1 on a saving throw against one of your warmage cantrips, it automatically fails the save and takes twice the number of damage dice dealt by the spell, as if you had scored a critical hit. The additional damage applies only to the creature that rolled a 1. Signature Focus​ Prerequisite: 5th level When you finish a long rest, you can place a unique sigil on a simple or martial weapon, which becomes your signature focus until you use this ability again. The weapon becomes magical, and you can use it as a spellcasting focus for your warmage spells. Your signature focus is bonded to you and gains the following properties. As a bonus action, you can call your signature focus to your hand, as long as you are on the same plane of existence as it. You can add your Intelligence modifier, instead of your Strength or Dexterity modifier, to attack and damage rolls made with it. Your signature focus has a number of charges equal to your Intelligence modifier, minimum 1. Once on each of your turns, when you deal damage to a creature with the focus or with a cantrip cast through it, you can expend 1 charge to deal an extra 1d8 force damage to that creature. The focus regains all expended charges when you finish a long rest. Snake Eyes​ Prerequisites: 10th level, House of Fortune If you roll a 1 or a 2 on a Fate Die, you keep the die instead of giving it to the GM. Unerring Strike​ Prerequisites: 10th level, true strike cantrip When you cast the true strike cantrip, you can concentrate on it for up to 1 minute. You gain advantage on the first attack roll you make against the target on each of your turns while you maintain concentration on it. Vanguard Rush​ Prerequisite: House of Knights Once on each of your turns, when you make a melee attack against a creature you can see, you can move up to 10 feet toward that creature immediately before making the attack. This movement doesn’t provoke opportunity attacks and doesn’t count against your movement for the turn.

Unlike other spellcasters, warmages learn only cantrips, which they pick from the following list as they gain levels in this class. Cantrips marked with an asterisk are described in full in this document; the rest are standard cantrips found in the core rules. If a cantrip appears on the wizard spell list that is not represented here, the GM can allow it to be a warmage spell as well. Acid Splash Force Weapon * Poison Spray Arc Blade * Frigid Blade * Prestidigitation Burning Blade * Light Produce Flame Card Trick * Lightning Surge * Quickstep * Caustic Blade * Mage Hand Ray of Frost Cheat * Magic Daggers * Shocking Grasp Chill Touch Mending Sonic Pulse * Cryptogram * Minor Illusion Springheel * Finger Guns * Moment to Think * Thunderous Distortion * Fire Bolt Phantom Grapnel * True Strike Force Buckler * Force Dart * The cantrips granted by an Arcane Initiation — dancing lights, druidcraft, message, sacred flame, shillelagh and spare the dying — are also warmage spells for you if your initiation grants them.

Each warmage is defined by their chosen House, which teaches them valuable skills and offers a confederation of allies they will keep for the rest of their lives. Five are named for the pieces of the board; the sixth is named for the wheel. House of Bishops House of Fortune House of Kings House of Knights House of Pawns House of Rooks

Dungeons and Dragons 5e’s Wizard has always felt underwhelming to me. Not in terms of power, mind you, wizards are certainly strong in their own rights. Nor in their flavor, the flavor of an arcane scholar and pursuer of knowledge is a great draw... However, the wizard’s ability to mirror that flavor mechanically has always felt less than adequate in my eyes. This overhaul of the wizard class aims to reinforce the wizard’s scholarly nature, along with giving them a sense of experimentation that was missing from the source material. After all, what’s a wizard without some crazy magical experiments to keep them occupied?

As a student of arcane magic, you have a spellbook containing spells that show the first glimmerings of your true power. See Spell Rules for the general rules of spellcasting and the Spells Listing for the wizard spell list. Use the 2014 PHB’s Wizard table where applicable. Cantrips At 1st level, you know three cantrips of your choice from the wizard spell list. You learn additional wizard cantrips of your choice at higher levels, as shown in the Cantrips Known column of the Wizard table. Spellbook At 1st level, you have a spellbook containing six 1st-level wizard spells of your choice. Your spellbook is the repository of the wizard spells you know, except your cantrips, which are fixed in your mind. Preparing and Casting Spells The Wizard table shows how many spell slots you have to cast your wizard spells of 1st-level and higher. To cast one of these spells, you must expend a spell slot of the spell’s level or higher. You regain all expended spell slots when you finish a long rest. You prepare the list of wizard spells that are available for you to cast. To do so, choose a number of wizard spells from your spellbook equal to your Intelligence modifier + your wizard level (minimum of one spell). The spells must be of a level for which you have spell slots. For example, if you’re a 3rd=level wizard, you have four 1st-level and two 2nd-level spell slots. With an Intelligence of 16, your list of prepared spells can include size spells of 1st or 2nd level, in any combination, chosen from your spellbook. If you prepare the 1st-level spell magic missile, you can cast it using a 1st-level or a 2nd-level spell slot. Casting the spell does not remove it from your list of prepared spells. You can change your list of prepared spells when you finish a long rest. Preparing a new list of wizard spells requires time spent studying your spellbook and memorizing the incantations and gestures you must make to cast the spell: at least 1 minute per spell level for each spell on your list. Spellcasting Ability Intelligence is your spellcasting ability for your wizard spells, since you learn your spells through dedicated study and memorization. You use your Intelligence whenever a spell refers to your spellcasting ability. In addition, you use your Intelligence modifier when setting the saving throw DC for a wizard spell you cast, and when making an attack roll with one. Spell Save DC = 8 + your proficiency bonus + your Intelligence modifier Spell Attack Modifier = your proficiency bonus + your Intelligence modifier Spellcasting Focus You can use an arcane focus (see the Adventuring Gear section) as a spellcasting focus for your wizard spells. Learning Spells of 1st Level and Higher Each time you gain a wizard level, you can add two wizard spells of your choice to your spellbook for free. Each of these spells must be of a level for which you have spell slots, as shown on the Wizard table. On your adventures, you might find other spells that you can add to your spellbook. Spellbook The spells you add to your spellbook as you gain levels reflect the arcane research you conduct on your own, as well as intellectual breakthroughs you have had about the nature of the multiverse. You might find other spells during your adventures. You could discover a spell recorded on a scroll in an evil wizard’s chest, for example, or in a dusty tome in an ancient library. Copying a Spell into the Book When you find a wizard spell of 1st level or higher, you can add it to your spellbook if it is of a spell level you can prepare and if you can spare the time to decipher and copy it. Copying that spell into your spellbook involves reproducing the basic form of the spell, then deciphering the unique system of notation used by the wizard that wrote it. You must practice the spell until you understand the sounds or gestures required, then transcribe it into your spellbook using your own notation. For each level of the spell, the process takes 2 hours and costs 50 gp. The cost represents material components you expend as you experiment with the spell to master it, as well as the fine inks you need to record it. Once you have spent this time and money, you can prepare the spell just like your other spells. Replacing the Book You can copy a spell from your own spellbook into another book-for example, if you want to make a backup copy of your spellbook. This is just like copying a new spell into your spellbook, but faster and easier, since you understand your own notation and already know how to cast the spell. You need spend only 1 hour and 10 gp for each level of the copied spell. If you lose your spellbook, you can use the same procedure to transcribe the spells that you have prepared into a new spellbook. Filling out the remainder of your spellbook requires you to find new spells to do so. For this reason, many wizards keep backup spellbooks in a safe place. The Book’s Appearance Your spellbook is a unique compilation of spells, with its own decorative flourishes and margin notes. It might be a plain, functional leather volume that you received from a gift from your master, a finely bound gilt-edged tome you found in an ancient library, or even a loose collection of notes scrounged together after you lost your previous spellbook in a mishap. Arcane Recovery You have learned to regain some of your magical energy by studying your spellbook.
